nOPOVJGH OF ST. lIELENS.—HER MAJESTY'S JUBILEE. At a meeting of the Town Council of this Borough, held on the 6th day of April, 1687, the following recommendations of the Special Committee appointed to report to the Council on this subject, were adopted. viz :- 1 That Her Majesty's Jubilee be celebrated 4a this Borough in bhe following manner : • 1. That &procession through the town to the Park be or- ganised, in which the local Volunteers. tr3e Fire Brigade. and the School Children be invited to join. 2. That on tho arrival of the procession at the Park the Mayor be asked to publicly name it " The Victoria Park." 3. Tbat a grant be made to each Elerunitary Day School represented after the rate of 6d. for each scholar in the pro- cession who is on the school register, for the purpose of providing refreshments for the children. 4. That a medal be presented to each scholar in the pro- cess:en. 5. That a dinner to 500 aged poor be given. 6. That there be a display of fireworks. 7. That refreshments be provided for the Voluntcers. Police, and Fire Brigade in the process'on. The Aldermen and Councillors for esch Ward will Act ad Local Committee for the collection of subscriptions to cove.r the expenditure, and donations may be paid either to them or to either of the local banks. V,Ortrp, • APRIL THE HANDMAIDEN. Let March have his say Faraday— Crack his cheeks as he blows Winds and snows Over valley and hill At his will: Let March have his say: But one day 'Mid his winds and his snows, Ere he knows, Ile will hear my feet As they beat On the dust of his hills; By his rills, He will see my face In its place, Through the mist and the dew , Shining through. .• "What you?" he will shout, "'Think to rout The lion in his path • And his wrath: You, the handmaid of May, Think to stay 4!! My will and my power t. In this hour?" Then on mountain and hill, r, Sharp and shrill, I shall hear the north Wind pouring forth In it's might, to o'erthrow And lay low Me, the handmaid of May, On my way. But swift I -shall leap, As from sleep, _ And blow from my mouth ' The sweet south, And drench the dry plain With my rain; I And to conquer at length All the strength Of my foolish fierce foe I'll let go • All the warmth of my soul, As I roll Back the Yell I had spun From the sun. Then I look for my foe, And, 10, Nor on mountain or plain Will he reign; But somewhither, somewhere, On the air I shall hear his "Godspeed and good day, 0 handmaid of May?" • NORA PERRY. ed 3 Mercury Svpplement.

The intelligent man, says Plato, will prize those studies which result in his soul getting soberness, righteousness, and wisdßrn. Sydney Smith once said that there were two modes of judging, of anything—one by the test of what has actually been done in the same way before, the other by what we can conceive may be done in that way. Most of the errors in judgment concerning the work of the world come from using only one of these tests without the other. Tact is, above all things, the most necessary for good manners. Tact implies quick observation and discern- ment—the power of doing and saying the right thing at the right moment and in the right way. Invaluable in every sphere, it is more especially a feminine quality, one also which plays an important part in both the social and domestic life of women, and through it, in a great measure, they wield their strongest weapon, in- fluence—a " right" essentially feminine and unassail-

able. ANswimisci PARSON.—A story is told of a catechetical address in which it was sought to lead a congregation of children to see that the wearing of a uniform was a mark of distinction. making the individual easily recognised and involving responsibilities. "You see a man walking -Try erect, dressed in a red coat—who is he ?" "A sol- dier, sir." "flight. Y:u see a man wearing a kind of helmet, and dressed in blue—who is he?" "A policeman, sir." " BMA again." Then the preacher braced himself up to sketch a parson. "You see a man dressed in a black coat, and wearing a stiff white collar—who is lie?" "A masher, sir," was the triumphant rejoinder. HURDY AND DESPATCEL—Among the many causes of poor and in inefficient work is the habit of hurry, which takes possession of some busy people. Having, or imagining they have, more to do in a given time than can be done properly, they grow confused, agitated, and nervous; and, under this pressure, they proceed with the work in hand without requisite deliberation and care, perhaps omitting parts of it, sometimes important parts, and producing at last an imperfect and inferior per- formance which can be neither permanent nor satisfac- tory. There is hardly any employment, from the sim- plest manual work to the most complex and difficult mental labour, that does not suffer from this cause. A NoiTxr, USE or ALL Foots' DAY.—The Duke and Duchess of Lorraine, when in prison at Nantes, in France, succeeded in escaping by making their attempt on the let of April. Dressed like peasants, one carrying a load on his shoulder, the other a basket of rubbish on her back, they both went out at the city gates early in the morn- ing. Here a woman recognised them, and ran off to alarm the sentry. "April fool !" shouted the man, think- ing the woman was trying to befool him, and so cried out all the other soldiers. When the governor heard the story, told him as a good joke, he got suspicious, and ordered inquiries to be made, and it was then found that the Duke and Duchess had really escaped, and were now safe from capture. The ladies in an Edinburgh congregation lately pre- sented their minister with a pulpit gown. The minister on the Sunday after it was presented, intimated to the people of the church, "The ladies have been kind enough to present me with a pulpit gown; but, lest any mem- ber should object to my wearing it, I shan't put it on yet, and will hear objections on Thursday night." Nobody came to object but an old lady. The minister said, Well, Janet, what objection have you to the pulpit gown ?" " Aweel, sir," said Janet, "we never read of the apostle Paul wearing a gown ?" The minister replied genially, "You are quite right, Janet; but then, you know, neither do we read of St. Paul wearing breelcs." That satisfied the old lady. He has also survived 21 Piesidents of the United States. i..A;iste,== ,i‘i-MiLitatiti= l PARIS BURGLARS AND THEIR ACCOMPLICES.—TIIO great 1 majority of the residents in Paris live in apartments, in all of which, large or small, the bedroom accommodation , is extremely insufficient. Servants' rooms are at the top of the house far away from the rest, and the result is that after retiring for the night they are free to remain indoors or go out as they please, their masters being none the wiser. In cases of emergency or illness this incon- venience is particularly felt ; nor is the system specially conducive to morality. But there is another side to the nuisance. Their employers are left defenceless against burglars; indeed, it is often found that servants are actu- ally in collusion with criminals whose acquaintance they had made in their nocturnal peregrinations at the conclu- sion of the day's work. A characteristic instance of this danger has just come to notice. A few days ago, a lady moving in good society there and occupying an apart- ment in one of the most fashionable streets in the Champs Elvgies quarter, received the visit of a police official, who informed her that at eleven o'clock that evening she was to be murdered, and her rooms plundered. She laughed at the idea, and the more so when the inspector proceeded , to ask her for particulars about her servants. Her butler ' had been for many years in her ernployment, her COOk the same, and so forth. Her own maid, who had come last, had been eight years with her, and thoroughly en- -3 oyedher confidence. Yet, to her amazement, the official explained that, this very woman was the accomplice of her would-be assassin. At last the lady was induced to isten to the voice of reason, and measures were arranged accordingly ; though she felt convinced that there was no ground for alarm. What was her surprise when, punctually at eleven p.m, after the butler and all the women, excepting the maid, had gone upstairs for the eight, a ring was heard at her door. The maid opened it, and told her mistress that a man wished to see her en particular and urgent business. The lady replied ttiat she could not see him at that late hour, but the ielajd returned with the message that the unknown visi- I ti3F insisted on an interview ; " i And look, madame," she! triumphantly exclaimed. "he is coming n." The man entered the room, and was advancing, in a threatening attitude towards the lady, when the inspector and two lwilicemen who had been cleverly concealed pounced upon ikina and took the burglar and the maid off in their cus- tEaY• The officers had been admitted by the lady, un- Illiven to the servants, a short time before. The plot been discovered by a policeman on his beat, who . heard a conversation between the burglar and the 1 51 in a neighbouring street, and followed the latter to house. The man was already known to the police as a dangerous criminal. But for the accidental discovery lki lady would have been murdered without anyone ifiting on her behalf. The burglar and the servant made a full confession. !Sisal. is RCMP* ? _ A good purse, a good cause, a good attorney, a good counsel, good evidence, a good jury, and good luck are the requisites for going to law. No one in anger is fit to estimate an offence or to redress a wrong; and he who attempts it is sure to have I cause for regret, if not for bitter repentance. "George Washington Napoleon Jackson Hannibal Harrison." "Yes, ma'am." " Tell Josephine Rosina Cleopatra Matilda Victoria to bring up the slop-pail." "Yes, ma'am.' It is best to strive to cultivate an interest in simple, innocent, and inexpensive pleasures. We may thus aid in diffusing that spirit of contentment which is of itself rich and a permanent possession. Harsh and unjust criticism of others' conduct or per- formance often results from using one's own ideal of ex- cellence as a test. A capable but captuous person ex- amines a piece of work or surveys a course of action, and sees, or thinks he sees, how it might have' been im- proved. At once he begins to find [fault, to depreciate, to blame, forgetting that the standard by which he judges his own, and not that of another. It remains at least very doubtful if he would have come up to it in the same circumstances; but to censure another for not bringing his practice into harmony with the censor's imaginings is surely unreasonable. Some years ago a certain Judge WU a candidate for Governor, and in making a public speech remarked, "Gentlemen, the office of Governor has been pursuing me for years!" Instantly a well-known character, Bill Arp, was on his feet asking to be allowed a question. The Judge declined to be interrupted. "All right," said William, with a shrug; "if you won't answer a question for one, these folks ain't going to vote for you, that's certain." "Well, go on, then, and ask your question," re- plied the Judge, snappishly. William arose. "You Say," he observed, "that the office of Governor has been pursuing you for years?" "Yes, sir." "Well, sir," said Arcli solemnly, "all that I've got to say is that you're gaining on it." Some seventy years ago, as the late Sir W. W. Wynn (grandfather to the present baronet) was riding in the neighbourhood of Wrexham, he heard a man sing in a cooper's workshop, with whose voice he was very much struck. It was Mr. Meredith, who possessed a splendid bass voice. Sir Watkin had him instructed, and he be- came celebrated as a singer of sacred music. He was engaged at the ancient concerts, oratorios, &c., but he resided chiefly at Liverpool. The following anecdote is told of him :_Having heard that a parish-clerk of a vil- lage in the Vale of Clywd, of the name of Griffiths, could sing down to double C, he.was determined to visit him. He accordingly started, and walked about forty miles. When he arrived in the village he inquired for Griffiths. A very little fellow, digging potatoes in a garden, was pointed out to him. "What !" thought Meredith, " that shrimp of a thing to sing lower than lean? Impossible!" Meredith was a fine, tall man, upwards of six feet high. He walked round the garden, eyeing poor Griffiths dis- dainfully; at length he said, upon low G, "Good day to you, sir." Griffiths, resting on his spade, replied, oi. double low C (five notes lower), "Good day to you, sir." Upon which Meredith marched off, with double C ring- in„g_in his ear all the way to Liverpool. WHAT Is "VEGETABLE MOULD? "—Vegetable mould is a mixture of the remains of plants with those of the I products of the weathering and decomposition of stone. Hence arise the different varieties of soil, its composition and consequent fertility largely depending on the char- acter of the mineral matter which makes up the rock upon which it rests, and of which it is for the most part the worn-down material. The thickness of the soil will also be regulated by the steepness of the ground from which it accumulates in a valley; along the side of a hill it is swept down not only by its own gravity, when it is not tenacious, but by the action of the wind, rain, and melting snow. The character of the soil is, however, altered by its being mixed with the decayed residue of the plants which grew on the surface; this residue, if rank, forms in time humus or vegetable mould. In some instances this is small, while in others, where the land is remarkably rich, as in the Black Earth Region of Russia, it will amount to as much as 12 per cent. Worms bore in and out of the mass in search of organic matter in the soil, and then venting the earthy material on the surface, add no small amount of finely triturated matter to the slowly gathering mould. Darwin, for example, noted in his researches on this subject,that during 29 years worms had deposited six and a half inches of castings on a single field. In centuries, at the same rate, the accumulation mustl have an important geological significance. In the tropics, the decay of vegetable humus is of course more speedy than in the colder north. Its decomposition and conversion into soil are expedited by the overflow of rivers, and the mixture of mud and other alluvial de- posits amongst it. Hence occurs the richness of "river bottoms," and, it may ha added, of drained swamps when the decaying vegetation has not been converted into peat. —Front" Our Earth and its Story" for April:

WYCLIFFE SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY, WARRINGTON.. On Sunday last special services were held in Wycliffe Church, and collections made amounting to £55 in aid of the Sunday schoole The Rev. J. Yonge preached two excellent sermons ; in. the morning from Psalm 34, 11, and in theievening from Matthew 17, 8. An address was delivered in the afternoon to scholars and friendoby Mr. Samuel Rigby, J.P., of Chester, and formerly of Bruche Hall. For many years Mr. Rigby held office as superintendent of these schools,and his-visit on this occasion was very gratifying to his old friends. Dia address, though brief, was full of good, and earnest counsels to old and young, and was thoroughly characteristic of himself. We were glad to see that Mr. Rigby appeared in good and vigorous health, and full of spirit and energy. In the course of his address he said there were young people present just creeping up into life and who wanted to knoiw how they could make the best out.. Well,. he would tell them, siker an experience- of at least fifty or fifty-five years, that the greatest enjoyment ever he had in his life—and he had hakl as much) as most folks—was in the Sunday school. He would tell them why. It was because he saw a lots of young people there who were the future men and women by whom he should be surrounded, and. he saw their minds unfolding and receiving the truths that were taught. Very likely. they were striving and striving hard—and it was a hard strife sometimes—to avoid what they ought not to, do and to encourage what they ought to do, and he-had always had hope that the result would be that by God's help they would overcome the evil propensi- ties of their nature. If they only strove and strove earnestly he could not tell them what they might be. All things were open for them if they made up their minds to avoid the difficulties of the way—to avoid sin, and if they strove to gain among other knowledge a knowledge of themselves.—During the afternoon service Sankey's hymns were used, and were heartily sung. The Sunday school choir, under 'the guidance of Mr. G. Wallington, junr., as con- ductor, and Mr. R. 11. Pearson, as organizt, gave a very creditable rendering of the Hallelujah chorus. We have special pleasure in commending in high terms the character of the psalmody at the morningl and evening services. The Choir was most efficient, and the organ was handled by Mr. Ilerbert Hankin- 180n, of Derby, in perfect taste and style, his cotnpaniments of the hymns and anthems being most admirable. The evening service was very largely choral, two anthems being sung, and a solo from the Elijah "Lord God of Abraham" was well and finely rendered by Mr. W. 11. Wallington. The solo was followed by the quartett "Cast thy burden upon the Lord," given by Mrs. A. Lane and Mrs. R. H. Pearson, Messrs. R. R. Pearson and W. H. Wel- lington. The congregations were good, that in the evening being one of the largest that has ever been seen in the church. The entire anniversary has been gratifying and successful.

A FOOTBALL CUP TIE DINNER. BY CHANG LUNG. I am anything but a glutton, and I am not much of an epicure. but I certainly can enjoy a good dinner as well as a good many folks, and I know that the majority of human beings are built after my pattern in that respect. The proceedings at a many social apd other gatherings would fall very flat were it not that a good meal com- prised part of the entertainment. Why, the feed is, oftener than not, the only thing that is really cared for. Fancy a wedding or a christening, or even a funeral, without the usual tuck in. In the two former cases it would be barbarity in the extreme, and in the latter the only redeeming feature would be absent. Then the dinner itself! What a diversity of opinion there is amongst diners as to what constitutes a good dinner, varying from the modest "steel ho'" that little Bill Mossop pretends to be satisfied with in Manchester on a Friday, to the more extensive spread of many courses that habit can almost render necessary to the self-indulgent. But whatever the quality of the dinner, if it is enjoyed, it has a very palpable effect upon the diner; making him better company and more disposed to try to please others than he would be had he not satisfied the wants of nature. But a good deal of the enjoyment of a meal depends upon the way in which it is served up. I have seen the humble penny bloater cooked and served in such a manner as has made my mouth water; and I have seen prime joints of meat so spoiled in the cooking and serving that they would almost have disgraced a savage. Myself and a few friends went for a long walk in the country one fine Sunday afternoon, some time since, with the avowed purpose of trusting to luck for our teas. There were ten of us, and we meant having a tramp over a stretch of country which was mostly moorland, and of course very thinly populated. We had tramped all the afternoon, and it had got close upon five o'clock when we made up our minds that we must be havipg something to eat, or our mainsprings would give way. We had passed nothing in the shape of a public-house for nearly three hours, but about a mile ahead wo could discern a building which we took to be a wayside inn. It was unanimously decided that if it was an inn we would have tea there whatever the price or consequences. Upon a nearer approach our conjectures proved to be right, and with big sighs of relief we entered and sat down. The landlady appeared to be an agreeable per- son, and quite chatty in her way. Being all of us staunch temperance men, we ordered single glasses of whisky each. While the landlady was gone for the drinks,.l said, "Let's play a bit of a joke upon the old woman by each of us putting sovereigns and half-sovereigns down to pay for our drinks." This was agreed to. I was nearest the door, and I put a half-sovereign on the table. The landlady came in with the drinks, put them round the table, and looked at the rows of gold coins for a second, and, without saying a word, picked up my coin and departed. I said, "She's going to fetch the coins one at a time, because she cannot trust to her memory. She's no doubt afraid of making a mistake." ?resentiv she returned with some change, and waited until I had counted it. I said, "Why there's three shilliegs too little here." She said, " Yo'n getten o as yo mon hey," and she walked out. There was a good deal of hilarity in that room for some time in which I didn't join. The little joke cost me three shillings; for everyone pocketed his coin and drank my heath. Upon asking our hostess what she could give us for tea, she said she lied some beefsteaks, " rale nahse uns as hoo were sure would suit us." .This was better than we expected in such an out of the way place, so we ordered them cooked without &lay. We congratulated our-- selves and each other a good deal on having been so for- tunate in securing a substantial tea, and with the pros- pect of the enjoyment of it before us, the gauge of our spirits rose till it indicated about sixty pounds to the square inch. ' Very soon a delightful sizzling was heard proceeding from another room, and a glorious aroma of frying meat filled the air. What with the walk in the country, the bracing air, and the smell of the cooking, we were get- ting nearly ravenous. We-had had our.. glasses replen- ished and were getting impatient when the landlady walked into the room with a fried beefsteak on each of her bare open hands, and looking triumphantly round; i said: "Isn't them nahse uns, newer?" Consternation reigned supreme. For a few seconclia. no one seemed capable of articulating a sound. Inquir- ing eyes were looking at first one and then another, then at the smiling woman win, the smoking beefsteaks spread on her not over clean hands, like a couple of het cakes. At %rigth one of the- party—a round-paunched,. happy-visaged member, wheee sense of the ludicrous overcame his disgust—burst into a guffaw that made the works inside the clock fairly rattle, and provoked such peals of laughter from the rest of us as made the woman think- we had gone demented. So astonished was she that she dropped one of the steaks on to the sanded floor; which caused such a renewal of the oachina-- tion as made her hastily pick up the steak and precipi- tately leave the room, After that, every time that the woman camein there was such laughing as I think had never been heard in that house before. When she-put the tea on the table she brought a large ill)? of pickled onions and a lump of cheese, besides the beefsteaks, which were in a large meat dish. There was a good deal of magnanimity shown over that tea. Errervbody was anxious to help everybody &he to the nicest steak in the dish, and everybody, with a. disinterestedness truly noble, denied himself to oblige his friend. But the cheese !: There never was such a &mand foe-cheese, and when that was finished &raid was made upon the pickles* which we sliced and made into sandwiches. After teaovhen the landlady remarked that we hadn't eaten any beef, we told her that the cheese and pickles had been so very good we had for- gotten the beef. It was a cruel situation for hangry men, but Ththink the fun fally compensated for the loss of the steaks. -.tie story above recorded has no connection with

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS. —MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15 p.m. LAND TRANSFER.

On the-motion of the LORD CHANCELLOR that the Land Transfer Babe read a second time, Lord.ininrota, of WARDOUR moved that the bill be read a. second time, that day six months. He thought thebilftwas_one that would affect the estates and families of every peer in that House. He had nothing to say against its proposals with regard to the transfer of land, buthe opposed the measure on the ground thatit went out of its way to abolish the law of primogeniture and entail. The Lonn CHANCELLOR, who-expressed himself grati- fied by the reception given to the bill, said the measure was-one which would be only appreciated by those who were concerned in matters connected with land, He denied that the expenseof land transfer would be greater under the bill than It was at the present moment, and stated that due attention would be paid to the valuable suggestions that had been thrown out in the course of the debate. If the bill should pass he would promise to bring in a bill for the purpose of consolidating it with other measures bearing on the subject. The amendment being withdrawn, the motion for the second reading was agreed to. The House adiourned at 7 40-p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS. —MONDAY.

The Sp-miter took the chair at 4 p.m. BOGIES PETITIONS.—Sir C. FOSTER, ELS chairman of the Committee on Petitions, brought up a special report from the committee, which stated that they had found a petition presented from 'Flaggerston in favour of the con- tinuance of the London co.- and wine dues, which he must describe as a "bogus one." This petition.contained some 400 signatures, which were evidently all written by four or five persons. This was a distinct parliamen- tary offence, and he had, therefore, to move that the order for the reference of the petition to the committee be ex- punged, and that the order that the said petition be laid on the table be read and discharged.—Mr. 'BRADLAUGH hoped that the House wquld take some stronger action. He had reason to know that money was being largely spent in collecting signatures-to such petitions.—Upon the SPEAXER'S suggestion the debate was adjourned for a week, in order that Mr. Bradlaugh might consider what steps to take in the matter. In answer to Mr. Sexton, Colonel ICmo-Hearmax said ' that in carrying out the evictions on the Skinners' estate, near Draperstown, county Derry. the sheriff was pro- tected by a force of 250 police, and on Monday last met with considerable obstruction,the police havingto disperse a mob with truncheons. In all 38 persons were evicted from six holdings. The authorities had no power to direct that shelter huts should be provided on the evicted farms.

Mr. tiosctrinkr, replying to Mr. 0. Morgan. said the number of publicans in the Metropolis who had been con- victed of sr 'ling' adulterated beer between 31st March, 1886, and 31st March, 1887, was 316. Ihe penalties amounted to £7,667, and were placed to the credit of miscellaneous revenue.

div.head: "THE PARNELL LETTER."
div.p: "THE PARNELL LETTER."

-- At the end of question time, Mr. SEXTON brought before the House what he considered a breach of privilege committed by Mr. Brodrick in a speech in the country, when he spoke of the fac-simile published by The Times as "Mr. Parnell's Letter," notwithstanding Mr. Parnell's emphatic repudiation of it. Mr. BRODRICE, in reply, avowed that he had so de- scribed the letter and left the justice of his description to the judgment of the public. Mr. SEXTON asked whether, after Mr Parnell had de- clared the letter to be a "barefaced forgery," it was not a ,breach of privilege to continue to attribute it to him, but The SPEAXER held that as the matter did not refer to , coeduct in Parliament there was no privilegein it.

div.head: BUDGET PROPOSALS.
div.p: THE BUDGET PROPOSALS.
The House went into Committee on the income-tax resolutions. .

Mr. GLADSTONE, who rose amid slight Opposition , cheers, said that a number of members were absent from I the House when the Budget speech was made, from the ; construction, or misconstruction, of the Chancellor of the Exchequer's remark, that it would be a hum-drum Budget; but whether for good or evil it would nnques- i ; tionably be remembered n future times, because it involved considerations and principles which entitled it to be remembered. His sincere desire was so to restrain the expressian of his own opinions as to make it a capi- ,tal object to avoid ,using any language which would raise any political difficulty during this, as he considered, preliminary discussion. The adoption of the proposals of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and the credit or otherwise of them. depended upon the Liberal Unionists. Not Content with a surplus of about £1,075,000, 'by one great stroke, :the nature of:which he would 'not now describe, the Chancellor of the Exchequer had raised that surplus to £2,800,000. He was disposed to agree with the minor changes of the right hon.. gentleman. With regard to the sum of £280,000 for England and •Scotland, and the 250,000 for Ireland, which was to be awarded to the local authorities in respect of 'the carriage tax, he con- fessed, he greatly regretted that proposal on the part of the Government. (Hear.) He admitted it was a pre- cise repetition of what was done by a Government -with which he had the honour to he connected, 'but it was done simply because they had to sub- mit to the will of the House of Commons. Be agreed with all that Lord R. Churchill had said on the question. The objections to that proposal were strong ; and manifold, but not because he thought the ratepayer ffid not deserve relief. The ratepayer was in a cruel position, and was ground between the upper and the ' nether millstone. In the last 30 or 40 years a new set of social and economic wants had come into force and great additions had been made to the rates, the ultimate bene- fit of which had gone entirely to the owner. That was a gross injustice, because the whole burden had been laid on to the occupier of ;the soil. As to the income tax , that no doubt was a boon which seemed to be given to hon. members as a sort of Easter offering or Easter due. He admitted that an income-tax at Bd. with no war on hand was discreditably high; but the income-tax ought 'to be reduced, net by a resort to resources which he did not think :legitimate, but by a wholesome and sound 'process of public economy.. He was not prepared to ad- mit that the reduction of the income-tax without that economy was a proposal which ought to be approved. As to 'the proposal for more than one Budget, he must point out that:the real control oi the House of Commons depended on the presentation of one Budget in the year. :If a number of different Budgets were to be made at dif- ferent times .of the year, that was a Misfortune which went to impair and even to threaten to destroy the con- trol of: the House of Commons.; but the most 'important duty of the Chancellor of the Exchequer was the duty to steadily work for the redemption of the National Debt. From 1868 to 18:4 the Government reduced more of the National Debt by the redemption of terminable annuities than haa ever been done. They were now asked to diminish the sinking fund, to reduce it in round numbers from £7,000,000 to £5,000,000 a year. When the income of the country was £900,000,000 or £1,000,000,000 a year, was this proposal worthy of Mr. Disraeli or Sir Robert Peel? Would either of them have approved of it, ,or would it recommend itself to the honour of the Conservative party? In the whole his- tory of the century no reduction bad ever been proposed , of the sinking fund corresponding with that now sug- . gested., if a large demand for a sudden expenditure arose, as might be expected to arise from time to time, a bold and just Government would persuade Parlia- ment, as far as possible, to meet that demand by taxa- tion; but it could not go all lengths for that purpose. 'What the Chancellor of the Exchequer now proposed was not demanded by the country; but it was only ingeniously concocted to meet the case. The right hon. gentleman said: "Let us reduce the sinking fund to a moderate ammmtand then we shall be safe:. But what was a moderate amount? Why should not another Chancellor of the Exchequer say: "Reduce it to £4.,000,000 ordo £3,000,000?" The wise and prudent man should be on his guard not to admit those beginnings, but bear in mind the admirable feeling of the Government of the country, which had completely recognised and approved this method of reasonable effort for the reduction of the National Debt. I Lord R:mmorrri CHURCHILL asked the House to allow , him to supplement the remarks he ventured to make last Thursday by remarks which he could assure the committee *ere in true friendship to her Majesty's IGovernment. He wonld come first to the tobacco duty, the remission of which he doubted the policy of at the present moment,-and he would ask whether the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer could depedd on this remission of indirect taxation? He thought it was only within the last two or three years at the outside that the in- direct taxes had produced the amount estimate& and he believed trade would be greatly disorgatused by the change. In regard to aids to local taxation, in the course of a speech on Mr. Pall's motion in 1883 for the relief of local taxation, the Chancellor of the Exchequer hoped the Hottse-would put its foot down against giving relief to local taxation without at the same time introducing a measure for the reform of local government. MR. W. H. SMITH AND HIS SECRETARY'S FULMINATIONS. Mr. Oxesw asked the First Lord of the Treasury whether it was true that in a letter addressed to the 'Bournemouth Habitation of the Primrose League, on Saturday last, he stated that he felt the necessity of passink the Crimes Bill as speedily as possible "So as to put an end to the tyranny and coercion of the loyal antl peaceful peasantry of Ireland by the National League, and to secure the punishment of these dastardly and cowardly assassins ; and whether he meant to convey by this expression that there is a connection between •the National League and aoc.essination. Mr. W. H. Siam; I have not seen the letter to which •the hon. member 'refers; but I am, of course, responsible for the act of my secretary, who informs me that his letter was in answer to a letter which contained a refer- ence to dastardly and cowardly assassins, and that the words used in his letter were apphed to t:iose men who had been guilty of grave offences against the peace of the country, and of cruel attacks on unprotected peasants. Mr. SEXTON said that the words of the letter of the right bon, gentleman's secretary seemed to imply a connection between the National League and assassina- tion. Would the right hon. gentleman address a letter to the Bournemouth Habitation in order to put an end to this false impression. Mr. W. H. Surru: I am not prepared to accept this representation of the.letter as accurate. I have not seen it,, 'but will take care to do so. THE CRIMES BILL. .0n the motion to go into committee, Mr. ROBERT HEm moved, as an amendment, that this House declines to proceed further with a measure for strengthening the criminal law again.st.combinations of tenants, until it has before it the full measure for their relief against excessive rents, in the shape in which it may pass the other House of Parliament. He contended that the tenants would be reduced by the Act to a position in which they would be unable to move hand or foot, the result bt4ng the renewal, on the part of the landlords, of that system of wholesale eviction which had always been so fruitful a source ot crime and outrage. The bill brought into the House of Lords wholly failed to provide a sirfficient remedy. Mr. &raw LEFEVER, in seconding the amendment, painted out that originally the bill was presented SS one directed against crime, but latterly Lord Hartington had said it was to put down an unlawful agitation, and recently the Prime Minister had said it was to put down combinations of tenants. Under these circumstances it was the duty of the House to wait and see what was the full measure of relief to be proposed by the Government.

Mr. A. RaLroun spoke of the wearisome nature of the debate, which in the opinion of the Government had already been more than sufficiently prolonged. He quoted from returns of outrage in Ireland, to show that while there had been a decided increase of agrarian crime in Ireland, there had also been an increase of ordinary crime, exclusive of the metropolitan district. Mr. GLADSTONE appealed to the Chief Secretary to fur- nish the House as soon as possible with a memorandum showing the principle on which the police had acted in classifying crime and outrage in Ireland,.and the dates at which any departures or changes in that principle bad been made, so that the House might have the means of instituting a comparison. Mr. A!, listvocut promised that such a memorandum should be drawn up. Lord Woman., speaking as a Liberal Unionist, re- marked that those who agreed with him felt that while their primary duty was to maintain the Union, yet in supporting the Government wth that object they in- tended to yo,• the utmost pressure on them to ensure the passage of a measure as would put an end to un- just and barbarous evictions. (Hear, hear.) Mr. E. HARRINGTON (Kerry) deprecated the spirit imported into the debates.—Mr. J. C. ELLis (Notts) supported the amendment, and attributed such disorder as now prevailed in Ireland to evictions and the dread of evictions. Mr. B. Wallace also spoke in support of the amend- ment. Mr. MONT:MLA, who likewise gave it his support, blamed the Government for the conspiracy of silence with which 'they were meeting the arguments urged against the bill. Referring to a recent speech of the 'Prime IMT:dater, in which the Crimes Bill and the Land , Bill in the House of LIP had been alluded to as being regarded by the Government as sister measures, he asked why the Coercion Bill should be reg:lrderi a the sister measure of a remedial bill. The Opposition recognised in the leaseholders' clauses of the Land Bill a substantial benefit, but the leaseholderaformed enly one- f mrth of the Irish tenantry, and for all the restthe mea- sure was nothing more than a cruel mockery. It was not intended as a measure of substantial justice, but to satisfy the English people and juseify the Government in bringing in a Coercion Act. The right hon. gentleman was proceeding to examine the. details of the Land Bill, whenrhe was called to order by the Speaker, and went on to criteise the Bill under immediate discussion, maintaining that the slate, of crime in Ireland was not such as to justify the Government in bringing it forward. Not only was it denounced by the majority of the Irish and English people, but also by the bulk of the intelligence and en- lightenment of America. Mr. Dir.low asserted that the framers of the Land Bill before the HOMO of Lords were totally and disgracefully ignorant of the condition of Ireland. He denied the. existencemf any such amount of mime, outage, intimi- dation, or combination in Ireland as would justifyllwr Crimes Rill. (Hear, hear.) THE TAUNTON ELECTION.-PETITION AGAINST

- • THE TORY FOR BRIBERY. The polling for the vacancy at Taunton, caused by the succession of the Hon. Charles Allsopp (Conservative) to the peerage, took place on Saturday, the candidates being the lion. Percy Allsopp (Conservative) and Mr. J. H. Sanders (Gladstonian Liberal). Crowds of voters were waiting at the various polling booths at the hour of opening, but, although market day, there was little ex- citement. Favours were freely worn, especially by the Conservatives, who anticipated a large majority. The official declaration was made as under :—The Hon. Percy .Allsopp, 1,426; Mr. J. H. Sanders, 890; majority, 536. The announcement was received with loud cheering by a large-crowd. At the last general election Mr. Allsopp was returned unopposed. In 1885 the polling was—All- sop? (C), 1,361; Sir Charles James Jesse!, Bart. (L), 978; majority, 383. The Hon. P. Allsopp addressed a crowd from the balcony of the Castle Hotel, and said that the ,news of his victory would resound from one end of the empire to the other, and show the country that the con- stituencies approved of the policy of the Government in their endeavour to restore order and respect for the law in Ireland.—The _Daily News says: "We are informed theta has been decided to present a petition against the return of Mr. Percy Allsopp for Taunton, and that the ne.inxy security has already been given. It is alleged on the Mere side that politics bad very little to do with the Conservative victory, but that bribery and treating had extensively prevailed." • A mass of evidence has been collected with regard to the alleged illegal practices at the Taunton election. This evidence will be submitted to counsel. The Liberal organisers took unusual precautions to obtain evidence of the alleged illegal acts by Mr. Allsopp's agents. Throughout the canvass certain gentlemen from head- 'iguartees in London were engaged in special inquiries in ccanzectice with this matter, and immediately the result , krflAsepelfwas known it was decided to lodge a petition 'agaleast-thasuccessfial canctidate.

there were many visitors to Stratford-on:Avon, which was decorated in honour of the occasion. The governors of the Shakspere Memorial Theatre have this year pro- duced.a revival of "The Merry Wives of Windsor," with new and elaborate scenery, specially designed and painted. The first representation was given on Friday night. Every part of the theatre was crammed, and hundreds were unable to obtain admission. THE QUERN IN A MONASTERY.—The Queen accom- panied by the Prince and Princess of Battenberg and suite, made an excursion on Saturday to the Monastery. of the Grand Chartreuse. The Father Superior received the distinguished ,visitors and conducted them through the entire building, special permission having been granted to show her Majesty the interior, which has I hitherto been closed to women without exception. The 1 monks had previously offered the Queen the hospitality l of the monastery, but her Majesty preferred lunching en route. . A determined attempt was made on Saturday evening to murder a woman at Dorking. It appeirs: that a man and a woman named Davies, who were supposed to be man and wife, had been in the town all day selling primroses. About six o'clock they entered the Black Horse Inn, in High-street, when a quarrel occurred between them, during which it is alleged the man stabbed the woman just below the chin :with a sharp table knife, inflicting a terrible wound. The man, who stated that he came from Marylebone, was immediately , taken into custody, and the woman was removed to the ' Cottage Hospital. SCHOOL BOARDS.—'There has been issued from the Education Department a blue-book on the subject of School Boards and school attendance committees in Eng- land and Wales. Exclusive of London, with its one ; School Board and population of 3,834,354 at the last I census, there are in the municipal boroughs of England 1 137 Boards, to a population of 7,010,172, and in Wel& i boroughs 18, to a population of 248,511; while in Eng- lish paristies there are 1,789 Boards to a population of 4,44%023, and in Welsh parishes 279 Boards to a popula- tion of 751,391, the total population under the 2,224 School Boards being 16,284,451. The number of English boroughs under school attendance committees is 116, with a population of 1,841,923, and Welsh boroughs 9, with a population of 40,478. The number of urban sani- tary districts under such committees in England is 73, 1 with a population of 821,593, and in Wales none. ACTION FOR BRICACII OF PROMISE OF MARRIAOM --fu the Queen's Bench Division, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Grantham and a common jury, an action for breach of promise was heard, the. plaintiff, Emma Horsman, 21 years of age, being a housemaid, and the defendant, rnest Burton, aged 28, a butler. Mr. Black-well was counsel for the plaintiff. The defendant did not appear, the plaintiff's counsel stating that he was understood to be in France, and that the action was undefended, the only question being as to the amount of damages. The parties became acquainted in 1884. They were in service for some time at Ryde Park Gardens and elsewhere. They had some corre- spondence by letter. The defendant at first wrote in very affectionate terms, but a change cameoverhim which he said he could not account for. He had made the plain- tiff an offer of marriage and it was accepted; but after a couple of years he broke off the engagement without giving any satisfactory explanation of his conduct. He had induced her to leave her service in view of their marriage, and before the engagement was broken off she had bought her marriage outfit. The plaintiff having even evidence fa that effect, her mistress, whose service she had left to be married and who had taken her back, testified that the defendant had always given her to understand that he was going to make the plaintiff his wife.—The !earned judge asked the jury to award such damara enlY as they considered fair and reasonable in the cirenmstances.—The inry gave a verdict for £5O, and his lordship gave judgment for the anaonat, with poet%

They do not even say that 4°Posal has any merit in their eyes; that w°°l(l carry it any if they could, or hold tsrlirarlY hope that it may be done in the riel4; their answer is, we repeat, a blank Atil.,-`l,ve• There is the usual talk about ;1110w-cial difficulties, as if it had not beegn: r 1 again and again that it is not a gue °f the way but of the will. Still, as there thtgreat amount of gross ignorance amongst 'i it n'2nts, may be advisable to show that SteltPon which they stand is exceedingly . The Deputation which met the Library that'ePllnittee began with the assumption ihat"' subscriptions were abolished, the worst tio ccAlld be anticipated was a deficiency of y Rrow°; 4rld then proceeded to show that hof rate, increase of fines, hire of h ec: room, abatement in gas, and suh scrip tthietyibliriacrhy Waswere promised on condition that made free, the whole defi- this theyeb3l,,,would be covered. More than, D --Inted out that they had allowed to i pass 44 tart Of the annual expenditure such items hire 21161) ris for painting, and special expendi- c:lo cleaning cases consequent upon the qee alterations—items which could not thilattr again for some years. The £4.0 or so to avallabl e could, it was urged, be apPnect, Par -Ing the cost of the extra wear and ,ql)r,°°llsequent upon the hocks in the '4llll-rY being for the first time brought into ths7. But notwithstanding kr the Committee cannot see their way; Itt,ltc "one are so blind as those who won't iht Lne Report which they have issued, tzti -wrary Committee suggest that the ulated • relied Increase on the rate is not to -044, on from the fact that the received this yeat "is £528, the same

as it produced in 1882, and only one pound more than the average of the last six years." This may be so ; but it is scarcely fair to take the average of six years of depression, during which there has been a reduction in assess- ments. Let them widen their basis, if they would make it trustworthy ; let them take an average extending over twenty years, and they will find that the average increase is, as stated by the Deputation, at the rate of Li+ per year. The £szB is evidently exceptional, for, on turning to the estimates for the cur- rent year, we observe that the penny is esti- mated to realise £540, which is indicative of an increase of something like the normal rate. As to the average expenditure, we do not attach any importance to the fact that the Library Committee make it out to be some Lso more than the sum named by the Deputation as spent last year. There can be no question that the Committee are perfectly capable of spending double the sum they ob- tain now—that is if they can get it—and that, too, without making the Library free. If they had been appealed to in 1867—that is twenty years ago—they would undoubtedly have said, as they say to-day, that the penny rate in Warrington, whatever it might do in other towns, would not permit of the rate- payers having a Free Lending Library. At that time they had to keep both Library and Museum going with a total income of £322 —namely, £2.5r from the penny rate, and £7l from subscriptions. The plea that they "couldn't do it" might have had some force then ; but what becomes of it now, when, , according to their own showing, their income has been nearly doubled? The amount received from the rate has increased more than 'co per cent. during the last twenty years, and yet we are still to be told that the contribu- tion from the ratepayers is not sufficiently large to permit of the Library being made free! With regard to the debit balance of £l7O it is sufficient to say that it is the result of the Committee having " overrun the con- stable" during the extensive alterations they have made. They managed last year to pay over £3OO of this extraordinary expenditure ; and if they could do that in one year, no one need be alarmed at the mention of £l7O. Besides, the Deputation indicated a course by which the debt might easily be wiped off. With regard to the last statement in the Report, that the towns mentioned by the Deputation were named •as cases parallel with Warrington, we are in a position to say that they were brought forward with no such object. They were mentioned to show that Warrington, compared with these Places, was exceedingly well supplied with books to begin with—that there was no ground for pleading that k here could be any difficulty about commencing a Free Library with ro,ooo volumes in the Reference oe- partment and iOOOO in the Lending Depart- ment. The fact is the Library Committee have made up their minds not to move; and we challenge the Chairman to say whether we misrepresent him when we affirm that he is opposed to the principle of a Free Lending Library. He acts, and some of the Com- mittee act, as if they were irremovable trustees of the Library and Museum. It is about time they were made to realise that they are nothing of the kind ; that they are simply the servants of the ratepayers; and that they hold office from year to year only. If the ratepayers desire that the Library shall be free —that Warrington shall be put on a level with every other town by which it is sur- rounded—they have a right to make it free. The Committee have a right too; they have the right to resign, if they do not feel equal to obeying the mandate of the ratepa7ers. It is absurd to suppose the matter can end with the adoption of the report of the Library Committee. That report will be brought before the Town Council on Tuesday even- ing; and the ratepayers will have an oppor- tunity—from the tvay in which it is dealt with by that body—of judging who amongst their representatives really represent them in this matter.

• MR. GOSCHEN is a striking example of the way in which evil communications corrupt good manners.' Up to the time of his joining the Conservative party, he was re- garded, to quote Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL as "the canonised saint of financial purity ; " but he has not been a member of a Tory Government for six months before he has sinned and come short of what is to be ex- pected of an average Chancellor of the Ex- chequer. His Budget, at the first glance, is rather attractive; and it sounds well to talk about reducing the duty on tobacco, and taking a penny off the Income Tax. That the Income Tax oughl to be reduced goes without saying; it is a discredit to us as a practical and commercial people, that we should be paying a high war tax at a time of peace. But the reduction should be effected not by ceAsing to Day a portion of our debts, but by reducing our excessive expenditure. As Mr, GLADsTorrE remarked, on Monday night, "there is something effeminate in leaving our public expenditure untouched and yet proposing the reduction of a tax which was put on purposely to meet the ex- penditure." It is not honest financing ;it is a bit of national thimble-rigging, of which Mr. GOSCHEN above all other men, ought to be ashamed. He has preached a good deal about the necessity of courage and virtue in the conduct of public affairs. The extension of the franchise to boroughs, and then to the counties was, he professed, a weak conces- sion with which he would have nothing to do; and he has put on a similar lofty air when taking a stand against Home Rule. It has been the same in matters of finance. So late as October, 1885, he said he would H never " subscribe to any proposal for throwing over " Gladstonian finance, Glad- stonian economy, Gladitonian views of expenditure, and, more than that, of na- tional retrenchment." What, never ? Well hardly ever, and, unhappily, he breaks his vows the moment he becomes Chancellor of the Exchequer; he falls from the path of virtue at the very first tempation. Anybody, as Lord R. CHURCHILL puts it, could secure a remission of taxation by making a grab at the Sinking Fund and taking Two Millions from it. Mr. GOSCHEN will have earned the proud 'distinction—if we may accept Mr. GLADSTONE as an authority—of having reduced the an- nual provision for the reduction of the , National Debt to a point lower than it has ' ever been before during the present genera- tion. "Well, what does it matter," the easy going may say, "we have got a penny off the Income Tax ? " It matters much; it is bad in principle—it is a bad precedent. It is surely a duty to do something towards pay- ing off debt; and when that debt carries with it twenty-one millions in the shape of interest alone, it cannot certainly be looked upon as doing a big thing to pay off annually seven million cc the principal. Mr. GOSCHEN thinks otherwise, or at any rate has yielded to a sudden temptation. He wants to have the credit of reducing taxes; but he has not the

courage to go the right way about it; he does not reduce the expenditure, he makes a grab at the Sinking Fund. We observed in our last issue that the Budget was hard on the memory of Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, and we note that Mr. GLADSTONE, on Mon- day night, gives point to this evidence of the ingratitude of the Tory party. He said "The last stage of the case is this : El hi, lit-ute ; you have invaded the Sinking Fund Of Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE ; you, the re- presentatives, the very men of his party, who were his colleagues in the Government which established this Sinking Fund." But what care the Tories for consistency? When were they known to have any qualms of conscience as to matters of finance? Since 1883, the Army and Navy estimates have risen £6,000,000 ; and it would seem that JoHNI RuLL is to be saddled with this as a per- manent burden, that is if he will stand it. ' Mr. GLADSTONE asked for eleven millions when it was expected that there would be war with Russia, and it was granted. It his gone—it has all gone into the rapacious military maw, and the cry is still that of the daughter of the horse-leech, "Give, give." How long ; oh, ye tax-burdened people—how long? How long will ye continue to throw pearls to swine? Is it not time to turn aside from the vampires and give the children bread? A change a great change is needed. What the nation wants is to be financed by a GLADSTONE not to be " jewed " by a GoscHEN.
"TOUCH AND GO." "Snow, snow, beautiful snow "—oh yes, "beautiful exceedingly ; " but, descending in this country at the stammer end of April, it is like dirt—it is the right thing in the wrong place.
•On Tuesday Lord Granville opened a Free Library at Hanley. When will somebody, lord or commoner, open a " Free " Library in Warrington?

Exchange is no robbery. Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., laid a foundation stone of a Jubilee Baptist Chapel, and received a silver trowel. He has since sent £5 to the Building Fund, and doubtless feels that he has had the best of the bargain.

" A great failure " is announced in con- nection with Messrs Short, S'iort, and Co., whose liabilities are stated to be about £50,000. There is no failure, however, as to the name What, under the circumstances, could be more appropriate than Short ?

Tkie Warrington Board of Guardians are to be congratulated on having secured the Rev. G. F. Roberts as chairman for another year. He is the right man in the right place. Unlike some chairmen, who believe that speech is silvern, he knows that silence is sometimes go!den.
There is hope even of Mr. Chamberlain. In his last speech he managed to refrain from speaking of the Liberals as Separatists. This is better—very much better—than gross misrepresentation.

The member for West Birmingham is still willing to do what he can to close the breach in the Liberal ranks. The way is very easy; Mr. Chamberlain's Charter is one of seven points. Let Mr, Gladstone acknowledge that he is in the wrong as to every one of these seven points, and the whole thing is done—how simple!

Earl Spencer was gentle almost to a fault with Mr. Chamberlain in his speech at Battersea on Tuesday night; but he did not fail to point to the weak place in the proposal to have two Parliaments in Ireland. He said : In Ulster, among the Protestants, ray belief is if it came to the actual point, and they know that Home Rule must be given them, they would prefer to join a large and important Parliament at Dublin rather than remain with a small Parliament at Bel- fast. They wished to help and support their Pro- testant brethren, the minority in the rest of Ireland, if such a state of things came about. There is no denying this. If the Ulster Pro- testants really fear the Home Rulers, it would be cowardly on their part not to stand by the Protestants who are outside Ulster and scat- tered over the rest of Ireland.

-- Referring to the Government Land Bill, Lord Spencer exposed its fatal defect in calm but merciless language. He said It lest altogether in the cold the honest tenants who may not have too large judicial rents. The only method by which they could get redress was by not paying their rent. They might then have an ejectment served ov them by their landlords, and if they became bankrupt they might get redress. That appears to me, not only unjust, but one of the most absurd measures ever proposed in Par- liament.

Last night, the Coercion Bill was dealt with in Committee of the House of Corn- mons. It is evident the Government, by making it retrospective, intend to use it for the imprisonntent of Irish members and others who have advocated the Plan of Campaign. The more its provisions are discussed, the more monstrous they appear; instead of bringing peace to Ireland it will produce civil war.

The First Lord of the Treasury didn't figure very well when he was called to account in the House of Commons, on Tuesday, for allowing his secretary, on his behalf, to couple the National League with a proposal to punish what were called "these dastardly and cowardly assassins." Mr. Smith is usually decent as to language; but on this occa§ion he was found to be of the Smiths— smithy.

There has been an outbreak of typhoid fever at Budworth; and from the report of the Medical Officer of Health, it would seem to be due to bad sanitary arrangements. It is curious how some of the fairest spots on the earth are in other respects the foulest. At Croft, for instance, there is a sewer by the road-side which is simply sickening. Some- body in authority should visit the place— with a nose.

At Greenwich, on Tuesday, Mr. Montague Williams was asked to impose a fine of los only in a case of adulteration of beer, when it was proved that the offender had offered hush money to the extent of X 4.. Mr. Williams said if he imposed such a fine "he would be looked upon as an idiot." So he did a sane thing; he made the fine one of £3O, on the principle that it should be the business of the law to make it easy to do right and hard to do wrong.

The millers and corn merchants of Dublin hav3 "resolved to agitate for an import duty on foreign flour to the extent of 5s per sack of 280 lbs." Don't they wish they may get it ? Why not ask in a direct fashion for con- tributions of 5s each from heads of families? At present the appeal runs thus—" Please, iMr. Public, do let us make bread dearer in

!order that we millers and corn merchants may take lago's advice and put money in our purses." Lord Egerton, presiding on Thursday at the Central Council of the Diocesan Con- ferences, urged the clergy to accept some compromise on the subject of tithes. It is to be hoped the Vicar of Warrington will, read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest. The Rev. William Monk, vicar of Doddington, has shown the way. He has returned to the farmers the whole of the extraordinary tithe collected during the last fourteen years. The reverend gentleman is a " Monk " of the right order.

RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL.—An energetic canvas of Runcorn has been made during the past few days, and up to the present upwards of £2,000 has been subscribed. The tradesmen of the town are the chief holders of shares The committee of the Co-operative Saciety have had under their cons!deration the advisibility of investing some money in the scheme, but no definite conclusion was arrived at.

ACTION AGAINST WIDNES MANUFACTURERS At the Manchester AfOIiZPS, en Thursday, before Mr. Justice Day and a common jury, the action, Proctor v. Gossage and Son., which was for an infringement f a patent, was heard. Mr. Yates, who, with Mr. Hopkinson, represented the parties, said they had agreed upon terms. Defendants had agreed to judgment for the plaintiff, £5 to be paid for each • machine, with costs. I RUNCORN AND THE QUEEN'S JUBILEE.—The committee deputed to consider the best means of celebrating the Jubilee of the Queen have met several times. It is expected that the feeling will be unaeimoua in favour of having Jubilee rejoicings on a large scale, and we understand that the ; committee will probably suggest to the public meeting shortly to be held that a cottage hospital will be the most feasible permanent memorial of the event. WIDNES FOOTBALLERS IX HEUEST.—A letter has been received by Mr. J. E. Farrell. of Widnes, from Mr. T. R. •Sutton, of the " Athletic News," asking him to play for his team against Salford, on Saturday, and to procure two Widnes forwards. Mr. Farrell has also been asked to play at Kendal, en Saturday, but will, we understand, be unable to accept either engage- ment, owing to an injury he received a few weeks ago to oee of his legs. The Widnes forwards for Mr. T. R. Sutton's team will probably be Hardman and Hughes. • ROBBERY IN • RUNCORN PUBLIC-Rown.—Before Captain Hazlehurst, yesterday. John Wilkinson, a sailor, was charged with stealing 19s fid belonging to Clara Marsh. the landlady of the Ellesmere Hotel, Regent-street—On Mon- day night the prisoner and another sailor named Jas. Fryer went into the hotel, and the latter ordered two drinks and placed down a sovereign. The change was placed upon the counter, but a doqutbance arising, Fryer attempted to separate the combatalts. and was struck on the face. In the meantime the prisoner picked up the change, and walked away. Tile prisoner was apprehended OQ Wednesday by P.C. Charlea Potts, and was remanded.—Mrs. Marsh did not turn up to prosecute, and the prison,r was discharged.

" MESSAGE OF SYMPATHY TO IRELAND."—CopieS of the "Message of sympathy' from the women of England to their less fortunate sisters in Ireland are being freely signed at Newton by ladies of the Liberal party. The forms have only been in quiet circulatioii since Wednesday evening, and already a considerable number of signatures are appended. MARRIAGE OF S/12. A. B. WALKER.—The "Morn- ing Post" announces that a marriage is arranged and will shortly take place between Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, Bart., of Osmaston Manor, Derby- shire, and Gate,acre Grange, Liverpool, and Miss Maud Okeover, second daughter of Mr. Haughton Charles Okeover and the Hon. Mrs Okeover, of Oke- over, Staffordshire. ' STABBING A STEPSON AT LEIGH.—On Thursday , morning the Leigh magistrates committed a man named William Hopkins to the -assizes for unlaw- fully woundingliis stepson, John Cohen, at Leigh, on the 9th inst. Prosecutor went home late on the above date, after which an altercation ensued be- tween the prisoner and his wife, prisoner threaten- ing Cohen. As the latter was leaving the house Hopkins struck him with a sharp knife, four severe wounds being inflicted, from which he lost a cen- siderable quantity of blood. _ _

THE LATE MR: SAMUEL ROWLAND, OF WN/TLEY. —There has been recently erected in Whitley churchyard a polished Norwegian granite memorial stone ,to the memory of the late Mr. Samuel Row- land, of Grimsditch Hall, Whitley, Cheshire, who was accidentally killed at Huddersfield Station some months ago by falling between the platform and a train which was in motion. The memorial stone, which has been erected at the cost of the widow of the deceased, is the work of Mr. Ephraim Aukland, sculptor, Warrington. THE NEWTON L/BERAL "300."—A specially con- vened meeting of the members of the Liberal " 300 " of the Newton Division was held in the Do-cperative Hall, Earle-st., Earlestown, on Thurs- day evening. There was a large attendance of delegates, among those present being Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P. (vice-president), who occupied the chair, bream. G. W. Rawlins (Rainhill), R. Yates (Golborne), P. Hall, L. T. Foulkes, F A. R. Neill (Bold), M. Birkhead, A. J:Rawlinson (Newton), and others. The business was not of a publid character, the matters under discussion relating to the finances of the association. Fox-TERRIER COURSING MATCH. About 500 persons assembled at the Star Inn- Grounds, St. Helens, on Saturday afternoon, to witness the fox- terrier coursing match for £25 aside, the best of 21 courses, between Thomas Milne's Bendigo, of St. Helens, and William Burrows's Handsome, of Sut- ton. There was a deal of money betted on the re- sult, Handsome being the favourite at guineas to pounds before the first rabbit was dropped, but Bendigo was in grand form, killing 11 to Hand- some's 4, thus winning the match by 7. The win- ner was trained by Mr. John Gerrard. St. Helens, and was in splendid condition. The referee was Mr James Gerrard. CHESENLE LINES PROVIDENT SOCIETY. The 12th annual meeting of the Cheshire Lines Plate- layers and Workmens' Provident Sick and Burial Society, which consists of the workmen employed in the engineering department of the Cheshire Lines Railway, was held, on Thursday, at the works, Battersby-lane. Mr. W. G. Scott, C.E., the chief engineer of the company, presided, and the meeting was largely attended by officials and dele- gates from various parts of Lancashire and Cheshire. —The Secretary submitted the annual report which stated that the number of members was 1,047. I large amount had been expended during the finan- cial year, 163 members having received assistance from the funds, while 19 death claims had also been paid. The report and statement of accounts having been passed. the secretary, Mr. S. S. Barton, and the auditors, Messrs. Duncan and Dale, were re-elected. The proceedings closed with a vote of thanks to the chairman. _ _

SHOCKING FATALITIES AT Sr. llBLinTs.—john Duckworth. a young man 17 years of age, and re- siding at 76, Fletcher's-row, Parr Stocks, died in the Cottage Hospital, on Saturday, from injuriesre- ceived while following his employment at Messrs. Baxter's chemical works, on the previous day. He was assisting other men to remove a principal on rollers, when by some means the principal fell on to the deceased who was crushed in a shocking manner. He was accordingly removed to the Cot- tage Hospital, where he died as stated. On Monday afternoon a collier named Ashall, 60 years of age/ and residing in Raglan-street, was instantaneously killed in the Alexandra Colliery, belonging to the St. Helens Colliery Company, where he was em- ployed. The deceased was in the act of filling his last box for the day, when four or five torn; of roof fell upon him. The poor fellow was buried for about two hours, and when the rubbish was removed he was found to be found to be quite dead. CONGREGATTONAL CHAPEL, FARTINGTON. On Tuesday evening a miscellaneous concert was held in the above-named place of worship in aid. of its renovation, and placing therein a new heating ap- paratus. The programme was an excellent one, the accompanist being Miss Kitchen, of Newton-le- Willows. Songs and duets were well rendered by Miss Kalthoeber.of Manchester; Mr. Piever Hughes, of the Manchester concerts; Mr. J. C. Nicholes, baritone, of the City Vocal Society; and all were, well received by a large and appreciative audience. Two capital solos wet e played on the violin by Mr. J. Woodcock, of Blakeley. In the absence of Mr. Cecil Berle, Mr. and Mrs. Charles Holt, of Parting- tion, gave with excellent effect "March of the men of Harlech," while Mr. Amer Woodcock and Mr. Caswell rendered the popular recital " Those girls at school." Votes of thanks by the minister, Rev. a Clegg, and Mr. Ambler, of Carrington, were given to all those who took part in the entertainment; to Mr. and Mrs. Groves especially, for getting up the concert, and Miss Timperley, Miss Rogers, Mr. Timperley, and Mr. J. Hagkerlev far aiding to carry it out to so successful a termination. Tnn LIVIMPOOL RICHTBITTON. —lt will be learned ' with much satisfaction that the Princess Louise (the Marchioness of Lorne) accepted the invitation of the Executive Council of the Liverpool Royal Jubilee Exhibition to take part in the opening '. ceremony on Monday, May 16th. The Marquis of Lorne will accompany her Royal Highness, along with several other persons of distinction. The Princess and the Marquisrhave already visited this city. While his lordship held the high office of Governor-General of Canada, he and the Princess embarked here for Quebec on three different occa- sions, and both en their departure from and return to this country, the citizens of Liverpool manifested the heartiest loyalty. • The visit of the Queen last I year stirred up the greatest enthusiasm, and this will be renewed in the welcome which Liverpool will offer to the Princess Louise. It is expected that the diSplay of armour at the Exhibition will be very fine. The Machinery Court will be filled with representative exhibits; the Life-saving Court will contain a complete collection of humanitarian ap- pliances for use on land and at sea; and the walls of the Picture Gallery will be covered with ex- amples of British and foreign artists who have devoted their attention to naval and military , subjects.

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT of the value of eyesight. In many instances when they first find their eyesight fail- ing, they purchase all kinds of inferior manufactured spec- tacles which in the end cause their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, Manchesier, and 143, Lord-street, Soiathport, has invented his" Perfection " Spectacles, which he adopts at either of the above addresses at is 61 per pair. He will guarantee that they are not to be equalled in the country for clearness coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight" free on apolication.—Advt. Mr. R. Verdin, M.P., was on Thursday re-appointed chairman of the Winsford Local Board for the ensuing year.

THE LATE Mn. EVANS, OF RIINCOEN.—At St.. John's Presbyterian Chapel, on Sunday, the Rev. Evan Williams, the pastor, preached a sermon having reference to the late Mr. Richard Evans, who was connected with St. John's Sunday School. Mr. Williams referred to the deceased's I valuable labours in the temperance cause. CAMDEN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The anniversary sermons were preached in St. Paul's Chapel, on Sunday, by the Rev. J. H. Goodman, of Hudderdeld. There were :good congregations at each service. At the evening service the National Anthem was sang. On Mon- day evening the pulpit was again occupied by the Rev. J. H. Goodman, in the absence of the Rev, J. Chalmers, M.A., of Liverpool. The collections in aid of the school funds amounted to .E5O 2a 6d.

THE BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A Boy AT Di^-rog.—At Wid- nes Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs F. H. Gossage and H. Wade Deacon. John Taylor, son of Thomas Taylor, farmer, Cow-lane. Ditton. was brought up on remand cliarged with having on Tuesday afternoon, the 19th inst, stolen with violence from the person of Joseph Smith, aged 13 years, son of the station master at Ddten Junction, a penknife and trowel.—lt was stated by both Inspector Wood and by the father, that the boy WAS still very ill and weak, and would not hi, able to attend court fora week. He was being attended to by Dr. McDonnell and Dr. McCain- bridge. The prisoner was remanded until Monday night. CRICKET.—Prescot v Widnes.—This match was played at Prescot on Saturday.
