THE THARSIS BULPIP'It AND COPPER COMPANT.—ThIi annual meeting of the shdreholdere of the Marais Sulphur and Copper Company, Limited. was held in Ulasgow on Thursday. Sir Charles Tennant, chairman of the company, presided, and in moving the adoption of the report said the market values of products had all sustained a serious fall, copper and iron ore to the extent of 10 per cent, and silver 3d per ounce. Such being the case, the reduction of 31 per cent. in the dividend was not a worse result than m.ght have been anticipated. The average dividend for 20 years had been 19i per cent. Until they got an improvement of a substantial kind in copper they would not expect to re- turn to their former prosperity. The net regult of the year's operations showed a hilance of £102,850, out of which they proposed to pay 71,- per cent, dividend, amount- ing to £88,099, and carry forward £14,750. The report was adopted.

FOOTUALL FATALITY AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at the Wid- nes Police Court. touching the death of Jahn Harrington, 12 years of age, who bad lived at 27, Wellington-street, with his father, Richard Harlington. chemical labourer.— The father deposed that on Monday, the 11th inst., the deceased complained of being hurt. There was a wound on his right leg below the knee, and as it became much worse. Dr. McCambridge was called in. Death ensued on the 23rd inst. Witness believed that inflammation set in.—By In- spector Wood : The deceased was not confined to bed men a week after he received injury.—John Ciarghan, aged 13 years, of 42, Cromwell-street, said he and the deceased and a number of other boys were playing football on 80t12.0 waste ground off Milton-street. The deceased said " Jack, I've got kicked come home," and he was limping, and witness went home with him. The deceased did not say he had been kicked wilfully.—Mary. Walsh of 44, Nelson-street, maid deceased told her that Thomas McCafferty had kicked him.—The foreman of the jury (Mr. Tallon) asked that medical evidence should be called before a verdict was re- turned, but the jury decided that this course was unneces- sary, and reconled a verdict to the effect that death re- sulted from an injury received while the deceased was playing football.

A WIDNES TRADESMAN ROBBRD.—At Eddishury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Hanley, in the employ of the London end North-Western Railway Company, was charged with having on the 5,1 March stolen seven Writing elates, valued at 2s 6d, and also with having received the same well•knowing them to have been stoles.—Mr. Preston prosecuted on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company. He said the defendant was in the em- ploy of the London and North• Western Railway Company and the Great-Western Railway, who were joint owners of the Birkenhead Railway Company. On the date in ques- tion certain slatea were consigned from Chester to Mrs. Hough, stationer, sf Widnes.. At Dunham Hill the train wae put in a refuge siding, near which place the defendant discharged his duties. Some of the slates were missed, and were found ultimately in a culvert along which the defen- dant went to his home. These slates were marked, and were afterwards found in the possession of the defendant. The Railway Company had to bring these cases before the public to show that they bad no desire to screen anyone of their servants who was guilty of an offence.—Mr. Brassey, who appeared for the defendant, said it had not been shown that his client had access to the culvert. His case was that the slates were brought to the house independently of the defendant, and without his knowing anything about them. His client had not a stain on his character. The defendant's eon found the slates in the culvert, and brought them home. When the police came the mothet was so fr!ghtmed that she told a lie, and said she had bought them at Chester.— The Chairman said they bad given the Matter their best consideration, and they could arrive at no other conclusion than that he was guilty. They considered the case a very bad one, and defendant would be sent to prism for one month with bard labour.

SALE OF WORK AT Wintivs.—A sale of work was com- menced in Hutchinson-street Primitive Methodist Chapel on Wednesday afternoon. 'Fite chapel was erected in 1869 at a cost of about £BOO. By persistent efforts the friends cleared off this liability, and then incurred a further charge I of £365 by the purchase of the freehold of the building. Of this sum £2OO remain, unpaid, and it was with the eb. jest of raising a portion of this amount that the sale was organised. There were a number of stalls containing the usual articles of a bazaar, and these were presided over hi, Mesdames Cooper, Snelson, Hoskin, Andrews, Carr, Apple ton, Pomfret, Atherton, Calved, Marshall, Worsley, and Hague; Misses Appleton, Carr. Baswett, Aidley, and Mar- shall. The refreshment stall was in charge of Mrs. Hill, Mrs. Aidley, and Mrs. Thomas Aidley ; and Mrs. Smith and Misses Newns, Walton,.Woreley, and Cartwright attended , to the tea ttbles. The children's • stall containing toys, &c, was under the superintendence of Misses Cartwright, , Worsley, M. Hoskin, M. Cooper, M. E. Smith, L. Smith. and Ireland. The young men's stall, which contained the model of a church, was in charge of Mr. Elijah Seddon, Miss Shingler, and Miss Ada. Marsh, of Runcorn, dispens.ad ice cream. The opening ceremony, on Wednesday, Was performed by Mr. Barnett Dutton, who delivered an ap- propriate speech. After remarking upon the pleasure it afforded him to be present, he said he thought they in Widness could not celebrate the Jubilee of the Queen in a better or more worthy manner than by clearing off the debts on all the chapels in the town and turning out the mortgagors bag and baggage. He adverted to, the admirable work carried on in that chapel, and wished them prosperity in all their undertakings The Rev J Calvert, superintendent ministeronnounced, amid applause, that Mr. Dutton had handed him a£s note—The sale of work was continued on Thursday, when Mr. S. Owens performed the opening cere- mony. In the course of a neat speech, he said he did not know what Methodists would do without sales of work. He should be glad to see something better enbetituted. so that the whole of the work would not devolve upon the ladies, and he was pleased to see the change that had been made in • the way of concerts. Sales of work, however, tended to bring together all sections of the Protestant community, and after all unity and love and faith were above all or- ganisations. The efforts now being put forward by the Primitive Methodists were very praiseworthy, and be wished them God speed in their labours.—lt was announced that Mr. Owens had contributed £3 35., and the statement was received with applause. Various amusements were pro- vided for visitors on etch day, and the performances of the Soap Works Brass Band were an attraction. The total amount realised WAS about £7O, which was considered very satisfactory.

r LORD WiNirAnimuri.—On Tuesday Lord Win- marleigh attained the eighty-sitth year of his age, having been born on the 26th April, 1802. His lordship, it is satisfactory to learn, is in the enjoy- ment of excellent health.

THE TITHE QUESTION.-It will be remembered that at a meeting of tithepayers in the townships of , Woolston-with-iMartirtscroft and Poulton-with- Fearnhead, held a short time since, it was deter- mined to petition the owners of the great tithes, the Master and Brethren of Earl Leycester's Hoe- viol, Warwick, and the owner of the small tithes, the Rev. W. Quekett, rector of Warrington, for a reduction of the tithes for the current year owing to the prevailing agricultural depression. These petitions were forwarded to their destination by Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, and in response the Master • aneßrethren of Earl Leycester's Hospital have di- rected a communication to be made to him, in which it is stated that havinggiven the matter of the petition due consideration, they had directed that I a return of 10 per cent. upon the amount of the tithe actually payable would be made to every 1 tithepayer of lOs and upwards who attended to pay hie tithe to the audits to be held in Woolston on Tuesday, the 31st May, and in Poulton on the fol- lowing day. It is said that owing to the illness of the Rector, the question of the reduction of small tithes is in abeyance.

WIDNES FREE. PUBLIC LIBRARY.
The annual meeting was held in Alforde Chambers on Wedneedav afternoon., Preseat—Dr O'Keeffe, Messrs H W Deacon, J.P , S Sadler, J Morrison, B Carey, and ST Atlien (Week to the Local Board).

div.head: APPOISTMITST O CHAIRMiIL
div.p: APPOISTMITST O CHAIRMiIL

• The Clerk intimated that this was the first business, and Dr. O'Keeffe said he had ranch pleasure in proposing that the chair during the ensuing year be takea by Mr. Deacen. Mr Deacon had always evinced a sincere and deep interest in educational matters, ad in everything that was for the benefit of the people of tha town,, and he theught the corn-1 mittee could not be preeiled over by a more worthy gentle- man. Irle hoped the successor the Library, which greatly depended upon the energetic action of the chairman, would be promoted to such an extent as to make Mr Deacon proud of the position he held..—Mr S Sadler seconded the motion with great pleasure, and it was carria unanimously.— Upon • taking the chair.. Mr Deseon said lie was glad to take the chair It second time in order to get the library into proper working order, but be hoped. his acceptance of the po-ition would not bo taken as a precedent for appointing the same chairman each year. TEE. 53NA5CIAL POSITION. The Chairman said that for the year ended the 25th March there was credited to the committee by the penny rate £4lO, making, with the donation of £lOO from Mr. J. D. Brunner, of Northwicb, a total of £5lO. Of that SUM they had already expended £2BB 13a I.d, which left a balance in hand of £221 6s Id. For the year 1887-8 they would obtain about £420 from the rate makivg with the balance a. total income of £641 to meet the requirements of the year. Mr. Allen had prepared an estimate showing a probable expenditure of £547 17s 2d on various small matters, leaving abort £lOO for books, and other expenses. He considered their affairs were in a very good position. Tar PROPOSED OPENING.

At the rcguest of the committee, thel-C-ha. irmari had writ- ten to Professor Rendall, of the University College, Liver- pool, asking him to perform the ceremony of opening the library. The reply was as follows :—" Dear sir,—lt would intermit me to be present at the proposed opening ot the

library, and to do anything in my power to contribute to the Bacons of the proceedings. So far as lam concerned, I should feel a postponement of the occasion an advantage rather than hurrying of it forward. As it m ekes no great difference as regards choice of night, I may say that all Tuesdays and Thursdays are engreeed. Other nights are indifferent, except for special engagements, and you will of course let me know before fixing vu any evening. I am. yours truly.G. 13.1tendall."—a brief discussion took place as to the form the ceremonysbould take. The Chairman thought that Professor Rsndall should deliver an address in the I Lacey-street Schoolroom or in the bathe, and then proceed to the library.—Mr. Carey considered that it... would be best for the professor to have a private view of the library first, and deliver the address afterwards. He further-suggested that the P.ofessor should be met by toe members of the School Board, the Local Board. the medical gentlemen, and other public gentlemen.—Ts subject was deferred to a future meeting..
SOMETHING THE PUBLIC SHOULD KNOW.

The Gloucester Journal of April 16th contained the tollow- lug remarkable statement from one of its readers : " Messrs. H. H. WARNBR dr Co., "47, Farringdon Street, London, E. C. "Garrnmanicr,—l would be neglecting a plain duty to my fellow man if, after the restoration of my health, when all Methods of the regular practice had been unavailingly need, did I not make known the means by which I was restored. I During the greater part of last year I suffered from acute kidney disease, pains and soreness, which finally became complicated with dropsy and severe asthmatic attacks. These latter became so bad that it was almost impossible for me to take breath, and the dropsy increased until the water pressed upon in lungs, almost preventing their use The kidneys refused to act as they should, and for a while I did not pass more than doze. of water a day. My condition was most deplorable I had the best medical advice that was to be obtained, who consulted with my regular medical adviser, a well-known and skilful man. They informed me that my water was full of albumen and tubecastsand gave me little or no hope that I should ever recover. My attending physician greatly relieved the difficulty I experienced in breathing, but my general condition gradually grew worse. At this time I was keeping the Nelson Inn, Southgate Street but was obliged to give it up. never expecting to return to business again. All these months I could not lie down on account of the asthma and dropsy, or rise from my chair without assistance, and for a long period was obliged to be assissted to dress and undress. On October 23rd, 1886 (a day I shall never forget),l had an unusually severe attackof asthma, which came near ending my life. My friends con- cluded I must die, and hurriedly brought in my family phy- sician. As all aid had failed, be saw no objection to lay using Warner's SAFE Cure, of which he had heard good re- ports. thouah never having bad any experience in its use himself. I also had heard of the great benefits derived from this medicine, but such was my condition that I did not like te use it without the sanction of my medical adviser. A bottle was obtained for me, and how thankful I am that it was. lat once commenced taking it and received almost instant relief. At this lime my breathing was so bad that it could be heard across the street I wasbloated from head to foot, and my water was thick with albumen. My physi- cian watched the progress of my We carefully under the use of Warner's SAVII Cure, using no other medicine, and each fortnight that the water was tested, we found the albu- men gradually grow less, until now I have taken 20 betties, and, thank God, all the albumen has left the water, the dropsy has disappeared, my breathing is natural, and I am at present well able to attend to bueimees, and am arranging to return to the Nelson lan. I can now walk miles with greater ease than I could do for years, and have no gout since I have taken Warner's SAFE Cure. I have had so i many inquiries regarding this medic ne, and its wonderful I effect upon me, that I write this lett,r, not only for the purpose of answering the inquiries which I am unable to do by letter, but to tell all sufferers from kidney or liver dis- eases to give Warner's SAFI( Cure a trial, and it will tell for itself. My recovery both to myself and my friends seems like a miracle, and I will gladly give any information that lies in my power respecting it to anyone. I am, yours truly,

"J. H. KILMINSITEH. "Band Master, lst Gloticester Fneineers, " Kingsholm, Gloucester." The remedy which cured Mr. Kilminster can be procured of all chemists and medicine vendors in the United Kinedom at 45 Bd. per bottle, or direct ef the manufac- turers, H. H. div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTOR BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Mom)Ay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Piekmere and

Alderman Hai-1.4015. MISCELLAI4I3OI79 —The followirg were dealt with for drunkenness: John Scanlan, in Buttermark4-street, on Sat- urday night, fined Sc and costs; John Barker, in Mersey- street, on Saturday night, fined 55 and costs; Thomas Griffin, and Margaret Griffin, at Pinner's-brow, on the 16th last, fined 5s and costs each.—Catherine Davies, for drunk- enness. and for assaulting P.C. Johnson, was fined 7s 6d and costs.—Herbert baviea, charged with working a horse that was in an unfit condition, was fined 21 6d including costs.— Two lads named Prince and Syers, summoned for stone throwing in the street, were each ordered to pag 18.— James Corker w ts ordered to pay costs, he having been sum- moned for furi9usly drilbing a horse and cart in Winwick- street. TrESDAY.—Before Alderman Webster. A DESERTER.—Thornas Bribe, a native of Eatontown, a deserter from the commissi triat transport corps, stationed at Woolwich, was remand.d to await an escort. THTIRSDAY—Before Major Litton and Mr. John Platt. DRITICKENNESS.—Patrick Lyons was charged on warrant with two offences by drstokenness in March, 1884. Defen- dant said that he was drunk for a whole week. (Laughter.) He was dismissed with a cantion.—Daniel Crosby was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road on the evening previous. The magistrates' clerk remarked that this was " Daniel's Jubilee year ;" it was his fiftieth appearance. FRlDaY—Before Captain Reynolds and Dr. Gornall. DIRITICIEENNESS.—Ernrna linwari, brought up for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street on the Previous afternoon, was sent to prison for seven days. She was re- leased from prison on Thursday, having been serving a week's imprisonment for drunkenness.—Jane Riley, for having been drunk and disorderly, and having assaulted P.O Westbead on tlis previuus day, was sent to prison for a

being a militiaman of the 6th Brigade of the South Irish Division of the Royal Artillery, did absent himself from the annual training.—Inspector Wood stated that on the 20th Inst. the prisoner was apprehended at Rainhill on a charge of begging, and was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. He informed the police that he was absent from the annual training of the Regiment, anti Superintendent Barker had since been instructed by the commanding officer to prose- cute the man.—The Bench imposed a fine of 40s and costs, or a month's hard labaur. THEFT OF COlL.—John Madden and John McCormick, middle-aged men, who lived in tha same house in Water- street, pleaded guilty to baying, on the night of the 25th instant, stolen 120Ibs. of coal from a wagon standing en the Canal Bank, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company.—P.O. Murray,who caught the prisoners in the act of committing the robbery, having given evidence, Inspector Wood said Madden had been twelve times before the magistrates, principally for drunkenness and McCor- mick had made sixteen appearances before the magistrates, and on one occasion was sentenced to three months' hard labour for stealing coal.—The Bench sentenced McCormick to three months' hard labour, and Madden to a month's hard labour. ALLEGED ROBBERY.—Thomas Eddowes, an elderly man, was charged with having, sometime during the past nine months' stolen a spade and a wheeluarrow, the property of Messrs Haskell, Deacon, and Co. The prisoner was for- merly employed by Messrs Haskell, Deacon, and Co., but left their service about four months ago. The articles were then missing, and were recently found in the prisoner's pos- session. Joseph Betney and Thomas Atherton ideatified the barrow and spade. The prisoner was remanded until Monday, but was released on bail. ANNOYING HIS MOTHER-IN-LAW —Martin Monaghan, a young man, was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Angel Hotel, Mersey-road, on Tuesday night.— P.C. Thompson deposed that be was called upon to eject the prisoner from the hotel as he was creating a disturbance,i and refused to leave when requested. When taken into ' custody the prisoner was most violent.—P.S. Robinson cor- roborated, and in reply to Mr. Lewin (magistrates' clerk) said Mrs. Sutton, who kept the Angel Hotel, was the pri- sener's mother-in-law, and he was coutidually annoying her. —lnspector Wood read a very black list against the pri- soner's character, he having served twelve months' hard labour for an attempted rape.--118 was fined 40s and costs a month.

1. IJGBY RULES. RuNcoaer v. LITELERLAND.—Runcorn were visited on Tuesday evening by a team designated as Litherland, but which might more properly he called a district team. The weather was very unpropitious, rain falling incessantly, but this did not deter a large number of spectators from assem- bling. The game was a very fast one, although Runcorn were the best all through, having the verdict at the finish of one goal, two tries, and four minors to one minor in their ' favour. Teams ;—Litherland.—R Ives, back ; Legge, Bal- mer, and Freeman, three-querter backs; Leadbetter and Larkin, half-backs; Holmes. R Wilcock,R Harding, Mur- phy, Fyles, Wilson, Russell, Houghton, and Johnston; , forwards. Runcorn.—Woods, back ;Lunt, Riley, and Caw- , ley, three-quarter bade; Andrews and Whitby, half-backs; ' . Wright, Wainwright, Ford, Faulkner, P Riley, Broady, , Dolan, Gatley, and Abram% forwards. I RUNCORN V. MR. H. H. BAINBRIDGE'S MANCHESTER TEAM —This special match, which was arranged by the Runcorn Football Club Committee on behelf of the Rancorn Gymnasium, took place at Runcorn on Saturday, a good \ attendance of spectators watching a most interesting game, , which resulted in a win for Runcorn by two goals, two I tries, and three minors to one try. The home team, who I were without H. Hughes, Wright, Daviee, and Speakman, had to call up from the reserve. The game was started by Haselhans, Woods replying, and play located about centre. Faulkner dropping well, the ball was taken up to the Man- chester line. Here Hughes gave Brody a chance, but Ball frustrated, and the ball travelled to Woods ; who by a huge kick sent it dead behind the visitors' line. Following the Idrop-out, a general effort by the home forwards again got the ball near to the visitors' lines, where W. Riley took a smart and successfull drop at ,r,oal. Haselham again started the hall, Broady replying, a mull by Wheeler causing play to settle in mid-field. Allen here got the ball from Moly- neaux and ran etronglv, Cawley and Woods stopping him, however, before he b came dangerous. Some long kicking by Wainwright and Bull followed the scrimmage, the bell ultimately falling to the forwarde. The Runcorn contingent took it towards the Manchester • goal, where Andrews snapped it up, and, brushing aside all opposition, landed over at the corner, and Broady kicked a capital goal from the place Haslel;am again started, and Molyneaux re- plied to Woods. Afterwards a short run was made by Allen, but he was stopped. From a line out near the visitors' line Whiltry, who bounded the ball in play, drop- \ped over the line, Bro.ody's kick at goal failing. The play from new up to half-time was in the visitors' halt, where strong efforts were made by Clarke, Broady, and Cawley to score. After changing ends the ball was started by W. Hughes, Broady smartly preventing a return, and Riley and Lunt making strong efforts to score. Some smart passing I by Donaldson, Allen, and Escourt now enlivened the game, a good pass out by Andrews afterwards giving Riley a chance to score, which he availed himself of. The goal- kick, however, again failed. Play having been resumed, by a strong effort the home quarters were gained by Moly- neaux, his effort being frustrated by Hughes and Galley by a nice dribble along the touch line getting the ball away. , Lunt and Wainwright n'ixt tried for an opening, but a for- fard dribble by the Manchester team took the ball on to the home line, Bainbridge scoring their first point. The kick at goal by Haselham failed. Hughes dropped out and Haselham put in a good run, bat this was I neutralized by a clever dribble by Clarke, which Wain- ' wright followed with a spirited run, but was overhauled by Donaldson. The game shortly afterwards ended in a win for Runcorn as stated. WARRINGTON V. MANNINGHAM. The list of fixtures of the Warrington Football Club for the season 1886-7 was brought to a close on Saturday by a' match with the well-known Manningham team, on the ground off Wilderspool Causeway. Much interest was mani- fested in the game, and it was witnessed by about 5,000

spectators. Ashton having won the toss Fawcett kicked off with the wind against the visitors at foul o'clock. Halfyard kicked to Massey, Toothill getting a free kick, and then the ball was sent to touch by Newton slightly in Warrington quar- ters. Barnes now intercepted a pass to Newton, pot in a nice run, but was tackled and passed to Massey, who trans- ferred hostilities to the visitors' quarters. The visitors, however, worked to centre. Warren getting bold pat in a nice ran, bat passed forward. The same player shortly afterwards pased to Evane, who tailed to hold. Massey kick- ing to touch. From the scrimmage near the centre Little- wood and Rigby broke away, and Davies finely tackled 1 Fawcett. Speakman put in a geed pass to Barnes, who re- passed to Evans, who pat in a nice dodgy run to 25. A miss I Iby Barnes let in Moson, Evans stopping. Clark, one of the , Manningham men, at this juncture had his shoulder pat eat, and had to retire to the regret of all present. Scrim- mages took place in centre for a considerable time, and, 1 Evans, on the ball becoming loose, kicked to touch. Bow- lands next led a dribble past the centre, Massey saving., The Manningham forwards, not to be denied, took the hall over the line, e minor resulting in their favour. Asburst . put in a nice run to touch from the kick out, and Moxon . was well tackled by Evans. Fawcett then put in \ kick to half-way. and Halfvard improved matters to touch. Warren led off with a dribble, Fawcett re- plying with a good run and kick. Play now raged on the Warrington line, Littlewood relieving, and then the Man- ningham 'forwards rushed the ball up the field and scored a minor. Ashton kicked our, Newton returning to touch. Again the Manningham forwards worked the ball to the line and compelled Warrington to touch down. Good play on le part of Fawcett...and Jones took the oval to the line, but the Warrington forwards relieved to centre. Midgley led a dribble to the Warrington quarters, Nevins saving and kicking to touch. Frank Turner came through from the line out, kicked, and Barnes and Rigby following up took play to the Manningbam quarters. Then the little centre passed to Ashton. the ball going over the line, a miner re- sulting for Warrington. Up to half-time there was no furthe; score, which stood at three minors to one in favour I of the Manningham team. Crossing over, Frank Turner kicked off, the ball going into touch. The Warrington for-I wards quickly took it to the line, Ashorst tackling Speak- man when looking dangerous. For a short time the Man- ningham forwards worked the ball to the centre. Barnes pasaed to Frank Turner, then to Massey, play again being On the visitors' line. The Manningham forwards packed well, and eoming through the scrimmage took play to the 25. The Warrington forwards replied by taking the ball back again, and Massey put in a strong kick for goal. Faw- cett replied with a good It.ck, and Barnes getting in a good run passed to Ashton. This player passed to Rigby, who got on to the line, but from the scrimmage in front of the goal post Warren got hold, and when just on the point of scaring stumbled, thus preventing a certain try to his credit. The same player next gave a long pass to Massey, who galloped over the line, Frank Turner failing at goal. .1/4 few minutes elapsed and Shen Barnes put in a dodgy run and passed to Ashton, and the forwards aiding him be quickly took it over the line, Frank Turner again failing to improve the point. Barnes was now seen at his best, his good dodgy runs excitieg shut e of admiration from the spectators. At the centre of the field Fawcet got hold and made a splendid dodgy run through the thick of his oppo- nents, thus landing a try; the seine player failing at goal. This brought about the end of the game, Warrington being the winners by two tries one minor to one try three minors. Neither team was at ite full strength, the visitors being short of two players on their arrival, whose places were filled by local rani, but the game proved to be an interest- ing one ftom the spec'atore• point of view. This was largely due to the fine play of Warren, whose passing from half back may be truly said to have'won the game. The home three quarters were also in good form, the new mill, Evans. putting in some very smart play occasionally. Warrington forward division were more than a match for their oppo- nents, Ashton, Rigby, Thornier and Davies doing particu- larly well. Amongst the Yorkshiremen. Fawcett was by far the most effemive man, and the manner in which he secured his try was deservedly applauded by the specta- tors. Teams :—Maoniughame Full back, W. H. Rhodes; three.

NEW BOOKS, &C. "Great Composers" is the title of the current issue of the Camelot Classics series, publishedlby Mr. Walter Scott. These sketches of the great musicians of Germany. France, and Italy, are from the pen of Mr G. T. Ferris, and they areledited with an intro- duction by Mr. William Sliarp. The book gives an interesting and discriminating account of the life and work of over twenty great composers. It is exceed- ingly readable, and is in every way a• good shilling's worth. Amongst the " Great Writers" issued by the same firm there is a "Life of Dante Gabriel Rossette," by Mr. Joseph Knight. A popular work of this kind was much needed, for, although the public are familiar with the name of Rossetti, there has been nothing hitherto to Satisfy those who were anxious to know how this poet-painter and painter-poet came to exercise so great an influence over so many eminent men. Mr. Knight places Rossetti before the reader as his friends knew and loved him, and the result is that the reader comes to know and love him too. In the Canterbury Poets series we have for this month "The poetical works of Alexander Pope (selected), with an introductory sketch by John Hogben." To those who are familar with this series, it is needless to say that Pope looks well in his new dress. Mr. Hogben's sketch is long, but it is not too long considering bow much the character and abilities of the poet have from time to time been discussed. He holds the scales evenly, and we. thus get some good criticism of Pope's qualities: but most readers will doubtless be beet content to tarn to the poetry it- self, in the belief that it will give theta a higher en- joyment than criticism can afford. The current issue of the "Manchester Quarterly" (published by Mr. John Heywood) is above its high average. The frontispiece is a fine engraving of a choice drawing by Mr. Ward Heys. Mr. Alexander Ireland contriontes a very thoughtful paper on "Books for General Readers ; " and Mr. B. Sager has a critical paper, "The Sonnets of Robert Browning." There are other well-written papers, and last, not least, Mr. Thomas Hay does his level best with "A Ports- herd from Palestine," with an illustration which he also furnishes. The remaining matchee of the first rotted in this compe- tition have been played this week on the Warrington Foot- ball Club ground. On Monday evening the Daliam-lane Amateurs beat Warrington Rangers second team by a try ' and four minors to two minors. The game was a stubbornly contested one, for although the amateurs were evidently too heavy for their opponents, the Rangers played a fine defen- sive game. At the end of the ordinary two thirty minutes' play, neither side had a clear three points to the good, which are necessary to win a game, and consequently a fur- ther period of ten minutes each way had to be played, dar- ing which the A:nateers managed to ran up their score as stated above. On Tuesday night there was an excellent en- counter between Warrington 2nd team and Sr: Paula let. Toe ground unfortunately was very slippery owing to the I rain which fell during the afternoon and evening, and spoiled the play to some extent. The two teams, hone ever, were pretty evenly matched, and the contest between them was a stubborn one, though Warrington 2ad managed to come out wieners by two tries and two minors against St. Peals one try and one minor. On Wednesday evenieg the competing teams were Warrington Hornets 2.1r1 and Warrington True Blues, and again a very evenly-contested game was the result of the encounter.. Some good passing was at times indulged in by both teams, and this made the game a more interesting One than that of the previous night, in which nearly the whole of the work was done by 1 the forwards. The Hornets 2nd showed a slight superiority throughout, and won by a dropped goal and three minors to a try. On Thursday night there was a good gathering of spectators to witness the concluding match of the first round between Warrington Wanderers and Stockton Heath, ' \ This latter team has formerly played under Aosociatim rules, bat for this competition it turned out under the Rugby code The game throughout was evenly contested, but it was evident that some of the Stockton Heath players were handicapped by their unfamiliarity with the game they were playing At times, however, they pressed their opponents, but the Wanderers played a stout defensive game, and in the end won by one try and two minors to two minors.
Quoth the Doetor—" Nevermore!
Merely this, and nothing more.

A WOMAN KILLED BY A Cow.—A Woman named Jane Williams, of Nantyglo, has been killed by an infuriated COW. She was passing through the streets of Brynmawr, when the animal tossed her in the air. div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

„ - Railway ticket-collector: You surely don't expect those two boys to travel for one ticket, naa'ain 2--She: Most decidedly I do. It's a twin. A literary man who recently tried the power of the human eye on a ferocious bull is recovering from his wounds and bruises, but has lost all faith in such mes- merism. There is a hint of unspoken pathos, a touch of patient suffering and resignation, in this birth notice: ”In this city, August 9, the wife of Win. Lea, of a son —not twins this time." A Social, KISMET.—" Bread-and-cheese-and-kisses " was the way in which the refreshments were announced at a young ladies' social in Detroit recently. And every gentleman present looked as if butter wouldn't melt in his mouth and wished he had never touched a cigar. But the kisses were only French confections, and not the genuine thing at all. . A Husrawn's Minim—How comfortable for a young wife to feel that her husband is a bountiful provider, and that she will never want for the necessaries of life. A newly-married man was recently directed by his wife to order some yeast, and not having a very well-defined idea of the article, he told the baker to send up ten shillings' worth. At nine o'clock next morning three men might have been seen tugging a cask of yeast up the front steps of that man's house. A doctor in Soho made a nerve and bone all-healing salve, and thought he would experiment a little with it. 1 He first cut off his dog's tail bad applied some of the salve to the stump. A new tail grew out immediately. He then applied some to the piece of tail which he cut off, and a new dog grew out. He did not know which _ . dog was which. RATHER !—Wife to husband: Mother wants, to come and pay us a visit, John; but I have written to her to say that just at present, while baby is teething, it wouldn't be convenient. If I give you the letter, will you remember to post it, my dear ?—Husband, with an air of perfect confidence: Well, I should rather say I would! • EXCHANGE or Ins.—Tin-Tun-Ling, a famous Chinese adventurer who died a few • weeks ago, was in Paris during the siege. One day, as he was passing along the street, two heroes, whose military cestume consisted of a dingy red stripe down their black trousers, said in his hearing, "Bali—that Chinese would be doing better if he were in Pekin just now !" "And you, gentlemen, if you were in Berlin," he returned simply, and passed on. A mild eld clergyman entered a restaurant in Chicago a nd seated himself at the only vacant table, opposite to a ferocious-looking foreigner all whiskers and spectacles. "I hope I am not intruding," said the reverend gentle- man. "Not at all," replied the other, with a savage leer; "but perhaps you would not sit there if you knew who I am. lam the editor of the Hock-Deutsche Anarchist Trumpet." "Never mind," said his re- verence ; I have been chaplain to a gaol for twenty years." , , . CAN HIS WIFE EXPLAIN 2—" I understand," said the agent, "that you want a burglar alarm in your house." "I did talk of having one awhile ago, but I've given it up." "They are a nice thing." "Yes, I suppose so; but they wouldn't help my case any. I am not losing anything now ?" " You—you— ' "I simply leave my pocket-book in the barn o' nights instead of my bed- room_, and I haven't missed a dollar for weeks." A BOY TO BE ENVIIID.—A 12-year-old schoolboy, who had to be called a dozen times in the morning before he came down to breakfast was roused from his matin- slumbers the other day by a loud clap of thunder, the electric bolt knocking a big hole in the roof of the house, going through the ceiling, splitting open the headboard of the bed, singeing his hair, and passing through the floor and out of the kitchen door. The lad partly opened his eyes, faintly murmured, "Yes, I'm coming," and immediately turned over for a fresh snooze. , " Ah," said a visitor to the Golden State, "this is a , strange country! There are all sorts of people here, and it shows how wild and marked are the vicissitudes of I fate." "Yes," returned his Californian friend; "people ' rise and fall here. I knew an English baronet who drove a hack." "Dear me! You don't say so?" "Yes; and I knew a German baron who keeps a bootblack stand." "It's incredible! But look up there. It's the most curious thing I ever saw ;" and the visitor pointed to a sign over an oyster-house which bore the legend," Peter Simple, F.R.S., ' and, underneath, "Oysters." "Bless , my soul! A Fellow of the Royal Society keeping an 1 oyster-saloon !" "Well, no; that's hardly so strange," I said the Californian. ‘" F.R.S.' doesn't mean 'Fellow 1 of the Royal Society; 'it means 'Fried, Roasted, and Stewed.'" Mr. Washington Irving Bishop, who has excited so much attention by what he terms his "thought-read- ing," has had many interesting adventures, and not a few amusing ones. While he was in Belfast he gave an entertainment in Ulster Hall, which caused a great deal of animated discussion among those present. During the evening, and after the successful performance of several astonishing feats, a temporary lull occurred, during which a rich voice in the gallery called out loudly, " Misthur Bishop, Misthur—" 'Well, well, what do you want ?" inquired the entertainer. "01 epos° yes can foind annething a man wants ?" "Well, I think I can—nearly anything." "Will yes foind somethin' for me thin ?" "Certainly." "Well, the morrow's Sunday,an'oPd like yez to foind me a moighty foine dinner." Mr. Bishop is authority for the statement that the hero of this occasion received a " goold" half- sovereign. "It was about the best advertisement that I ever had," said he. MIXED Hoserraury.—A certain worthy clergyman in the North who was as much given to hospitality as his, good wife was the reverse was called upon one after- noon by a reverend gentleman. As they had been fellow-students together, and had passed their examina- tion before the same presbytery, they had of course much to talk about. One tumbler therefore followed another, and each tumbler brought along with it some- thing new to discuss, till the time arrived for the stranger to mount and proceed on his way. This however the kind host would not listen to. His heart was warmed and fully awake to the pleasurable feelings of sociality, and, in spite of all the nods and winks and dark looks of his wife, he insisted that his ; friend should remain for the night. This arrangement ' being effected, supper made its appearance, and was, as usual, followed by another tumbler by way of a "night- cap." Before retiring, the good dame was asked by her husband to bring in the family Bible. She started on this duty, and while gone the guest took off his shoes, opened the room door, and placed them out in the , passage-way. While stooping for this purpose, with his 1 head through the door, the good wife returned, and, I mistaking the bald head of his reverence for that of her ihusband, she raised the sacred volume and brought it down with a hearty rap and a matrimonial whisper— ' ." There—that's for garrin' him stay a' nicht!"
WESLEYAN SCHOOL *EXTENSION, AT

• ' PENRETH. On Saturday afternoon the foundation stones I, were laid of a large addition ,to the existing day I and Sunday Schools at Penketh. The accommoda- tion has for some time been felt -to be inadequate for the requirements of the neighbourhood, and an extension, the estimated cost bf which is about £9OO, was decided upon. Several sums of Money were promised towards a building fund, and recently a bazaar was held in the Bold-street Wesleyan School at Warrington, in aid Of the same object. Mr. W. Owen, Warrington, is the architect for the exten- sions, and Mr. Lloyd, Warrington, the builder. At 2-30 in the afternoon, the scholars, teachers, and friends met at the Sunday School, where a proces- sion was formed. Headed by Gossage's (Widnes) brass band, the membeis of which gave their ser- vices, they then marched through the village, the !ceremony of laying the foundation stones being proceeded with on their return. Amongst those present were the Rev. G. E. Young, the Rev. J. H. 'Jones, and Messrs R. Cook, R. Garnett, D. Garnett, B. Hobson; J. C. Routledge, Auklaad, Watson, Ate. After singing and prayer, four foundation atones I were laid by Mrs R. Garnett, Mrs D. Garnett, Mrs ' R. Cook, and Mrs Fildes (Stretford), each of whom contributed LI to the fund. A number of bricks were, also laid by the children. After the ceremony had been concluded the Rey. G. E.Young said that he rejoiced that the stones had now been laid. For a great many years the people of Penketh had toiled on in connection with educational work in both day 1 and Sunday School. They had been greatly encour- aged, but toundtheir machinery was not equal to the demands made upon it. It therefore became I necessary that they should make considertible ex- tensions, which ihey were endeavouring to do. They were very anxious to take care of the children and to train them up in the nurture and the ad- monition of the Lord, to teach them such lessons in early life as would affect their entire future, and which they would never forget. They wanted the young people to grow up in fear of God, to be ,pre- served from bad habits, and from unbelief, an to make them good men and women. They were do- ing a great work, which deserves the generous sym- pathy ot their friends. He hoped that the build- ings would be raised without any accident happen- ing. Mr. Robert Garnett, in the course of a brief address, said that the people of the neighbourhood would be glad to hear of the extensive alterations and additions that were about to be made to the school that had done so much good and valuable work. They wanted to leave the world somewhat better than they found it, and one way of doing that was to establish the means of education throughout the land. They were doing something towards that end in Penketh. A collection was subsequent- ly made, and in the evening a meeting was held in the school-room.

Here we have a library, about four-fifths of the support of which is derived from rates, levied upon all the ratepayers of the town indifferently, but from which only a comparatively few individuals—who pay a subscription which they can afford, but which some others cannot—Are allowed to take books home. THE IRISH UNDER-SECRETARY AND HOME RULE. Sir,—For the information of your readers I send you the following resolutions framed and adopted with others by the Irish leaders in consequence of a meeting held in the Bilton Hotel, Dublin, on the 19th May, 18,0, and which meeting was attended by all the leading public men of Ire- land, irrespective of politics or creed, and including Col. King Harman, the newly appointed allistant secretary of Ireland, who, I observe, admitted at Ramsgate, on Tuesday week, that he was a Home Ruler in 1570, but that Home Rule then was different to Home Rule now. Perhaps some ef eur local Primrose Knights will be able to explain to the dull Radicals of Warrington where the difference lies between these resolutions and the principle of the late bill of Mr. Gladstone's Government. 1. This aseoeiation is formed for the purpose of obtain- ing for Ireland the right of self-government by means of a national parliament. 2. It is hereby declared as the essential principle of this association that the objects, and the only objects, contem- plated by its organisation are : To obtain for our country the right and privilege of managing our own affairs by a parliament assembled in Ireland, composed of her Majesty the Sovereign and her suc- cessors, and the Lords and Commons of Ireland. To secure for tharParliament, under a federal arrange- ment, the right of leeislating for and regulating all matters relating to the internal affairs of Ireland and control over Irish resources and revenues subject to the obligation of contributing our just proportion of the Imperial expendi-

tore. To leave to ato Imperial Parliament the power of dealing with all creations affecting the Imperial Crown and Govern- ment, legislation regardiag the colonies and other depen- dencies of the Crown, the relations of the United Empire with foreign states, and all matters pertaining to the defence and the stability of the empire at large. To attain such an adjustment of the relations between the two countries without any interference with the pre- rogatives of the Crown, or any disturbance of the principles of the constitution.—You,

THE IRISH QUESTION. Sir,—lt was very strange that your correspondent falsely signed "Unionist" in his reply to my letter of the 9th inst., should have entirely put aside every argument that advanced in reepense to his invitation as to the course the Liberal Unionists were going to take in the present crisis Well, as one who is not ashamed to be called a Liberal Unionist, I was determined to give bun my views of the situation, and I think I may safely come to the conclusion that what I stated has been sufficient, both to convince him that the statements were true, and that they were impreg- nable. I clearly pointed out that Mr. Chamberlain had gone as far as he possibly could do at the Round Table Conference to bring about the re-union of the Liberal party. Mr. Chamberlain entered into arbitration with openness and candour, and etated his objections in an upright and straightforward manner, and although Sir William liar- court has told us in plain language that they were agreed on the main points, whilst those on which they differed were few and secondary, still they have allowed the nego- ' Mations to fall through. I well remember to My sorrow that when they were sitting around this table Mr. Sexton wade a violent speech and attacked Mr. Chamberlain. in a slanderous manner, and threw out the hint that they were not going to have any concession from Mr. Chamberlain. Now, lam inclined to believe that the hitch which Mr. Chamberlain said there was somewhere lay in the violent speech of Mr. Sexton. It would be taken as the combined opinion of the Nationalist party, which means that if the ' Liberal Unionists enter into arbitration with Mr.Glacletone, it is simply tieing Mr. Gladstone as the sole agency of Mr. Parnell and his pasty. In my opinion it was a great nals-1 take for Mr. Chamberlain and Sir G. Trevelyan to enter into the Round Table Conference at all. I am pained beyond measure to see statesmen like Lord Hartington. and Mr. Chamberlain, and Sir Henry James, cast away like men of straw in order to obtein an unholy alliance with such men as Messrs Parnell, Biggar, and Co, backed up as they are by Patrick Ford and Frank Byrne, and others from America. and yet " Unionist" beco.nes alarmed because the Liberal Unionises stand aloof for the present in supporting Mr. Gladstone's schemeavh.ch ie to hand over the government of Ireland with executive powers to such men as these, who are the declared enemies of this country, and who will have the power, if Mr. Gladstone's measure was to become law, of electing their own judges, and magistrates, etc., which every true-hearted Liberal would object to. We believe that Mr. Gladstone's measure, if passed, would bring about the very opposite result which he is anticipating if his measure was to be- come law. In fact, I truly believe that the Parnellites themselves believe the same thing. It is a matter of im- possibility for the Irish leaders, who are, in my opinion, the greatest politicians in the world, to accept a bill like this as deal, that could not possibly work unless they were pre- pared to adopt a precedent which the American colonies of last century rebelled against by refusing to pay taxation without representation, and which ended in the battle of Bunkers Hill that brought about complete independence. If Mr. Gladstone's measure became law, Mr. 1)&11101 would soon bring forward the precedent of the American colonies. It is not the question, as your correspondent asserts, that Irishmen are not qualified to govern their own but whether we are to maintain a Urited Kingdom, giving Ireland the same power as England, Scotland, and Wales; fall representation, and such an extension of local govern- ment as will enable the Irish to have control of their own purely domestic affairs, consistent with the safety of the Empire. I am sure that if such powers were granted, and the Irish leaders would make up their minds to give such a I system a fair trial, coupled with a radical change in the I land question, a great deal would have been done to bring ' about that contentment which has so long been absent from the Irish people. For your correspondent to charge the real Unionists with ignoring the present and past dissatisfaction in Ireland, is simply stating that which is not true. Had we adopted that course, we should very likely have looked through Mr. Gladstone's schomo like your correspondent. Imagine the Glarlstonians going about stumping the country about the bad government of Ireland. If this is so, how comes it see- ' ing that they have so long held power Is it not saying in effect that they are incapable of goverming the country, and that the Irish members are in a position to govern more effectually than the British Government? Would evictions for ever cease if Mr. Gladstone's measure was passed ? Would there be no Crime? Would there be no cause to have a law to maintain law and order? Would the low price of agricultural produce bring more money into the pockets of the DM farmers if Messrs. Parnell, Healey, Biggar, and Co. had the Government under their own con- trol ? Have the latter greater sympathy with the Irish ,1 people than the Liberal Unionists? Have they even so mnch ? I doubt it. lam sorry your correspondent should have adopted the lines which others like him have done, viz., to misrepresent Mr. Bright, especially after he has so often answered them. See his answer to the Rev. J. Sherlock two or three weeks ago, which I think he must have seen Then, again, in 1872 the same misrepresentations with regard to Mr. Bright being in favour of Home Rule, took place in the county of Kerry. The result was that the O'Donoglme wrote to Mr. Bright, and this Was the reply :—" Rochdale, January 22nd, 1872. My dear o"Donoghue,—lt is said some persons engaged in the canvass of the county of Kerry have spoken of me as an advocate of what is termed Home Rule in Ireland. I hope no one will venture to say anything so absurd and untrue. If it has been said by anyone of any authority in the county, I shall feel obliged if you will contradict it. To have two representative legislative assemblies, or parlia- ments, in the United Kingdom would, in my opinion, he an intolerable mischief. and I think no sensible man can wish for two within the limits of the present United Kingdom who does not wish the United Kingdom to become two or more nations entirely separate from each other.—l am, very truly yours, John Bright." In conclusion, let me say that I hope yolr correspondent will be satisfied that Mr. Bright has never been in favour of Home Rule, and in no case has he given expression to that effect. With regard to the charge of being a Coercionist, I can very well looked over, because I support an emancipa- tion bill which is destined to give liberty to the thousands of poor Irishmen who are facing such a system of coercion by the National League that is a disgrace te any civiliKl country.—l remain, yours respectfully, A REAL UNIONIST.

THE WAYWARDEN FOR FRODRHAIVI LORDSHIP. ' At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday. before Lord Tollemache (chairman), Hon. W. F. Tollemache, Messrs. CI 1 F. Wilbraham, J. Higson, S. Woodhouse, E. A. Wrigh , and IL L. Smythe, Mr. A. Fletcher, solicitor, Northwich, applied on behalf of a namber of ratepayers of Frodsbara , Lordship to ask their worships to appoint a waywarden for that township. A meeting of the township of Frodsham Lordship was held on the evening of March 24th. and that meeting was attended by a number of ratepayers. Two persons were proposed as waywardens of the township, ens being Mr. James Percival, a larae farmer and ratepayer, of God's Croft, and the other being Mr. J. H. Hargreaves. a small ratepayer. He woo nominated in opposition to Mr. Percival, and the allegation made by the ratepayers who brought forward that matter was that there was something like a packed meeting, and when a show of hands was taken by the chairman a majority was declared by him in favour \of Mr. Hargreaves. The persons who had supported Mr. Percival demanded apol of the township; but the chair- man, who was a supporter of Mr. Hargreaves, refused to allow a poll to be taken. No election of waywarden had ireally taken place, and he asked their worships to exercise the Dower conferred upon them under the Highway Act of 1862, and appoint Mr. James Percival as a fit and proper person to fulfil the office of waywarden Mr. Thomas Hadfield said he was present at a township meeting held on the 24th March last at Frodsham Lordship. He proposed Mr. James Percival as waywarden, and the Chairman. Mr. G. H. Daubs', clerk to the Widnes , School Board, proposed Mr. Hargreaves. The meet- , ing was held in the bar parlour of a public- , house, and there were ratepayers and non-ratepayers , present. On a show of hands being taken, Mr. Elargreaves . was declared elected. A Protest was made and a poll de- manded, but the Chairman refused—The Chairman: Had he a right to refuse you ?—Mr. Fletcher: No, he had not.— Mr. James Percival, the gentlem in who had been nominated to serve as wavwarden, was called, and a memorial was here 0 put in.—The Chairman said the magistrates had decided to appoint Mr. Percival as waywarden.

Sir Jehn Mellor, formerly one of the Judges of the Queen's Bench, died on Tuesday night at Dover, after a short illness, in his 78th year. In the action for libel brought by Lady Aylmer against the" Dublin Evening Telegraph," the jury, on Tuesday. found for the plaintiff, damages £250 and costs. Sentence of twenty years' penal servitude has been passed at the Central Criminal Curt upon a collarmaker named Fenimore for the man-laughter of his wife at Fins•
bury. All hope is now abandoned of the safety of the large Liverpool ships Inversnaid and Malabar, which are posted at Lloyd's as" missing," with their crews, numbering to- gether 53 men.

_ HOME RULE FOR IRELAND. Sir,—Will you permit me a short letter in your paper, as I think it is time for all good Liberals to speak out boldly, especially Irishmen, to pretest in the most emphatic man- ner against the drastic law of coercion, by which a Tory' Government tries to enslave a brave race of people who have by every honest means in their power every right to fight constitutionally for Ireland's freedom The Govern- ment ought to compel Irish landlords to spend a fair pro- portion of their large and exorbitant rents amongst the poor industrious tenants. But what do we see every day since this wicked and cruel Tory Government came into office? Nothing but all kinds of bad legislation for poor unhappy Ireland; nothing but assisting bad landlords to evict the Irish people, to send them from the land where their forefathers drew breath across the seas in thousands to make way for some foreign and false adveaturers. Sir, when I find since the Tories came to power Ireland has been drained of a quarter of a million of her beet sons and daughters, what does all this mean? I would ask some of the Chamberlain deserters to explain. Look to the way the Tories intend to rule Ireland 30000 sbldiers, guns and bayonets to match. 30,000 policemen, 17 20.000 pensioners, f t 11 12,000 informers ready to sell anybody, besides all the Castle backs and under-strappers. I honestly think it is time to get shut of this monstrous army, and plant the flag of Home Rule after centuries Of oppression. We hope and pray that Mr. Gladstone may live long to lead us all to victory, and bring peace and contentment upon our native land, and unite Great Britain and Irel.nd in a stronger bond of unity. It is not Coercion and Crimes Acts that the Irish people want. As Mr. Gladstone stated in the House of Commons, the present reign has been the most disastrous since that of Elizabeth, as the following statistics will show :—Died from famine in Ireland in this reign, of which we are now celebrating the Jubi1ee,1,225.000 persons; persons evicted in Ireland, 3,668,000; number of emigrants, 4,186,000. The great bulk of these emigrsnts,l of course, have gone to America, and then people are astonished to find that there is sympathy in America for Ireland. Mr. Gladstone went en to say that those four millions and a quarter of emigrants have produced since they quitted the Irish shores wealth to the amount of £685,000,000 for the benefit of the country they bays adopted, besides all the money they 80 kindly send to their friends and relations in oppressed Ireland, I might venture to say £2 000,000 or £3,000,000. But the land sharks de• veured it, as they are doing so to-day'. I, as an Irishman, strongly pretest against all kinds of coercion, and against Joseph Chamberlain's mode of dealing with the Irish nation and its people. Let him mind Bir- mingham, as Lord Randolph is prowling near it.—Yoars, . PHILIP O'BRIEN. 38, Navlor-street, Warrington, April 23rd, 1887.

THE ATM OF SOCIALISM. Sir,—The Socialist parties seem very busy just now. It may be that hard times are peculiarly good times in which to sow the seed of Socialism amongst working-men. The Chartist of fifty years ago had a very different state of things to fight against to that which we find to-day. In those days it was no ea,sy thing for mien like Ernest Jones and Thomas Cooper filo carry out. their life's werk. An active propoganda could only exist by those engaged in it daring to run the risk of ntonths' and years' imprisonment. To-day, with a few exceptions, no man need see the inside of prison gates. We have freedom of speech, and perfect freedom of combination ; a free press and a perfectly free platform for political purposes. There only wants a perfect knowledge of the immense potential powers contained in these things to enable working-men to brush away at once and for ever the shackles they yet wear. The Socialists have so far proved that, like all other parties, they are but human, and can lee as unsocial as any ether class of men. Split up under half-a-dozen different leaders, they have also half-i-dozen different papers through which their views are filtered to the people, and woe be to the man who dares to differ from them. I should think there mast be a few Socialists of to-day who are acquainted with the Socialist literature of forty years ago. If so, they will know what a source of weakness it was for every man to allow his ambition to override his good sense. The aim of each Socialiet,then, as now, seems to have been his own personal glorification, and his highest ambition to fling dirt, satisfied that some of it will stick. I find papers (headed "Justice" the most unjust and the most unmerci- ful in their dealings with the hardest-working of our public men. Other papers take to themselves a word we -should all reverence—" Freedom," and straightway preach- ing Anarchy and the complete abrogation of the rights of man. Working far the "The Commonweal," Mr. William Morris. with all the poetry of his nature, alone seems to hold in his hand the olive branch. " To-Day " requires the united tabours of all parties. The harvest is full— where are the reapers? And now, sir, what is the aim of the Socialist? Put in a very few words; he labours to drive out misery and poverty fern this beautiful world of ours. Can any man find fault with this object? Surely it is far more cern- mendable than to sit down with folded arms muttering "the poor ye have always with ye." But the greatest of all questions is, how is it to be done ? We have seen to what and how our Parliamentary system has grown. Huge and unwieldy', it devotes a very larce portion of its time to clearing off the statute books old and selfish class-made laws. One can scarcely-hams a law passed or a bill pro- moted during the last half century, the object of which has not been, indirectly, repeal. So we go on doing one slay what we undo the next. To this the Socialist answers "Just eo t" and straightway acting on this conviction he pro- nounces at once against all Parliamentary devices as so many shams, intended only to lull the people to sleep. In the slams of London, the Socialist gathers around him men, who, like famishing waives, are ready to Buse at any argument which he may fancy will lead to food, shelter, and clothing. Let a red flag be but unfurled, ard he will follow it anywhere or anyhow, so that it leads him ont of his present trouble. Same in the north ; the Socialist lec- turer is engaged with the colliers now on strike, irstilling into their minds that "the representatives of labour, instead of standing up for theirielectors, were merely obeying the orders of the wirenullers, and never uttering one vigorous protest against the unjust demands of the employers." I insist upon it that whatever may be the aims of S-cialists, those aims will never be gained by undermining the MA.- dance of electors in labour representatives. Mr. Hyndman calls tame' the "capitalist dogs to surren- der." Why, be might se well call upon the sun to stand

ANOTHER SHIPPING DISASTER.-18 LIVES LOST. I A New York telegram says that the schooner Flying I Scud, bound for Alaska from Kodiask, has capsized in the Shelikoff Straits. Eighteen men perished. A RUSSO-GERMAN FRONTIER INCIDENT. Pews, netukr.—The "Soleil" to-day announces that ' an incident of a serious character has occurred on the Sile- sian frontier, where a Russian sentinel who attempted to Prevent a German from crossing the frontier was disarmed by some Germans. THE ARREST OF A FRENCH OFFICIAL. A telegram from Berlin to the "Republique Fraoctise " on Friday morning stated that the order for the release of M. Schnaebele Was despatched on Thursday evening to Strasburg. Despatches received in London, both from Berlin and Pailst agree that M. Scbnaebelle has been released, but no direct confirmation has been yet received from Metz. THE DESTRUCTION OF A FISHING FLEET. LATEST DETAILS. With regard to the announcement that the pearl fishing fleet had been wrecked by a hurricane off the north-eastern r coast of Australia, Mr. Streeter, of New Bond-street, London, who is the main organiser of the pearl fishing industry in those waters, confirms the pews. Barnes, the captain in command, had telegraphed as follows:—" Hurri- cane dismasted both schooners; five loggers and forty other craft missing." The fleet was in the Indian Ocean, off the north-west coast of Western Australia, prebebly about fifty miles from the land. The schooners are from 100 to 150 tons burden, and the luggers would accommodate about thirty men each. , Altogether there would be between three hundred and four hundred men in Mr. Streeter's fleet. About ten per cent. of • the men would be white men, the remainder Malays and the other natives. The loss will be considerable, as neither of the vessels nor their contents would be in- : sated.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at 4 o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—Lord ()snow, in replying to Lord Harrowby, said her Majesty's Government Were seriously considering certain modified proposals by the Canadian Government for a rabsidy for new mail route to China, Japan, Via Vancouvers Island.—Lords Carnarvon, Dun- raven, and Granville strongly supported the new mail service.—A bill dealing with rabies in dogs, introduced by Lord Mount Temple was read a first time.--The Lord CuANcF.LLoR said, in reply to the Duke ef Marlborough, that the Independent Mutual Brethren Friendly Society frauds were under the consideration of the public prosecu- tor.--The report of amendments on the Railway Rates Bill was discussed, and the House adjourned. Mr. Stuart Wortley, replying to Mr. P. Stanhope, said the Home Secretary had not mita any statement regarding the action a the Ladywood district, at Birmingham, of the Primrose League. On clause 1, which provided ter a preliminary inquiry in cases when the Irish Attorney-General had received infor- mation that lose of life was to be apprehended in a pro- claimed district, although no person charged was in cus- tody, Mr. Manunt moved an amendment to provide that it, should be sworn information.—After discussion the amend- *sent was withdrawn, and a suggestion of Mr. H. HEALY moved an amendment to strike out the ward offence and insert the word crime in its place. Helhought action should only be taken where crime was apprehended.—The ATTORNEY. GENERAL submitted that offence was the proper word to retain in the clause.—Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT said that everybody knew what the word crime meant, but the word offence was very wide. It was as well that the House should know at once whether the Bill was to be directed against serious crime. The popular impression in the country was that it was a bill against crime, and crime did not mean small magisterial offences.—The SECRETARY for IRELAND objected to substitute the word trims for offence. If it was worth while to give summary jariscliction to magistrates to deal with offences, it was worth while to give them power of holding inquiries for the discovery of offences.-Mr. CHANCE said statements made by witnesses at preliminary examinations might as the clauses stood he need against them afterwards.—After some discussion Mr. DITToN objected to give resident magistrates power to in- vestigate petty offences on the oath of single policemen. The Irish Government would have power under the clause to sweep hundreds if people into prison who had been guilty of no crime —Sir W. HARCOURT said it was nowc clear the bill was not simply one for prevention and punish. meat of crime, bat that it was a measure imposing on the people of Ireland for ever penalties for new offences created by the bill by men who were not lawyers.—Mr. T. HEALY warned the Government that if the bill applied to minor mad trivial offences the people as a body would refuse to come into court, and gaols would be filled with prisoners for contempt.—Mr. GLADSTONE pointed out that the Govern- ment had wilfully wasted two hours and a half, according to the Irish Chief Secretary, discussing a point not material. If the Government were of opinion there win not a material difference between "crime" and "offence" why did they nut agree to the amendmeat? B. Balfour, Mr. Usher, and others insisting if it was it had never been exercised within the memory of living men.—Mr. T. Firralies amendment was rejected by 157 to 120 —Dr. Coy-antis moved an amendment to provide that the clause should be confin-d to offences committed after the passing of the act.- The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for Ireland opposed, and said the clause had been purposely drawn so as to apply to offmces committed before the pas- sing of the Act —Mr. T HEALY supported the amendment, and said the Government, it appeared, intended to do that which the law of England had always looked on with ab- horrence, namely, to pass a law to deal with State offences. It was intended to smash up the National League, but they would simply be putting their hand into a hornet's nest. It was report( I from Glasgow, on Thursday, that Mr. Sims Reeves is seriously indisposed from a severe cold. Lord Kinnaird died early on Tuesday morning, at his London residence. He was 73 years of age, and had long been in failing health.

ZTFIE FREE LTBR A.EY iTTEMON. - We append the report of the Library'and Museum Committee on the question of freeing the Warring- ton Library. It will be considered by the Town Council at its meeting on Tuesday. We comment on the report in our leader columns. THE REPORT. The sub•committee appointed at the last meeting, baying reported the results of their conference on Tuesday, the 19tti April, 1887, with the deputation of the Jubilee Com- mittee, on the subject of a Free Lending Library, and the committee haying discussed and considered the same do agree upon the following report : The present reliable income of the Museum and Library, accepting the figures of the &octagon, is 1.553, composed of the annual rate producing £532 and sundry receipts such as fines, &c., The expenditure, also according to the figures of the deputation, is £655. Therefore there is an annual deficiency, upon these figures, of £lO2, which has hitherto been made up by the subscriptions of the book-borrowers. The means of meeting this deficit suggested by the depu- tation in case the Lending Library were made free are as

follows : Estimated annual increase in the rate Suggested abatement in the price of gas to be made by the Corporation lO Suggested additional rent obtainable from the lecture room Estimated increase in amount of fines en detaining books I Suggested subscriptions ef borrowers residing out of the borough Suggested voluntary annual subscriptionsl...... --• £99

As to the estimated increase in the rate as a matter tr` fact the amount this year is £528, the same as it produced In 1882, and only one pound more than the average of the • last six years. Whether subscriptions could or should continue to be received from borrowers residing outside the borough; the committee are not prepared to say. The amount set down under this head, is, of course, conjectural, whilst the volun- tary contributions suggested would form at best a precari- ous and uncertain source of income. Without, therefore, going.further into detail, the com- mittee have to regret their Inability to adopt the views of the deputation. But the committee cannot accept as correct the figures of the deputation as to the annual expenditure. Passing by the accounts for 1885-6 and 1886-7 as abnormal, on account of the extraordinary expenditure on alterations in those years, they find that the annual expenditure during the seven years, 1878 to 1885, averaged £7o9,and the committee are of opinion that this sum as an average, instead of £655, is the lowest upon which the institution as now coustituted can be efficiently carried on. There is, therefore, a deficit of at least £154 per annum, instead of £lO2, to be provided for, if the subscriptions be given up. The committee also believe that if the Lending Depart- ment of the Library is made free, considerable additional expense will necessarily be incurred in various ways, and, until a satisfactory arrangement can be found to meet the whole difficulty, they are not prepared to incur the respon- sibility of so complete an alteration in the present system. A suggestion having been made that books for a Free Lending Library might be provided by means of an auxili- ary subscription department, the suggestion has been dis- cussed and the committee consider that such an arrangement would not provide for the necessary expenditure on binding or replacement of worn-out books, on periodicals, nor on certain classes of new books, and that it 'would not even, if successfully carried out, affect the position as above stated. As bearing upon the practicability of making any change which might increase expenses at the present time, the com- mittee note that at the close of the financial year at Lady Day their account showed a debit balance df £l7O, whereas in an ordinary state of affairs there should be at that date a balance to credit of at least an equal amount. The Report concludes with a tabulated statement of particulars as to several other Free Libraries which are said to have been "quoted by the Depu- tation as parallel cases." We learn, ho Never, that this, unintentionally, misrepresents the matter. The figures were quoted not to show "parallel cases," but to emphasise the fact that, compared with many other towns, Warrington is exceedingly well supplied with books for the purposes of a Free Library. ANTI-COERCION DEMONSTRATION

AT EARLESTOWN. The Liberals of Earlestown and district held a mass meeting in the Viaduct Institute on Saturday evening to protest against the Coercion Bill intro- duced into the House of Commons by the Goverr- ment. There was a very large attendance, and the proceedings were of a most enthusiastic character. The chair was occupied by Mr. G. W. Rawlins, of Rainhill, who was supported by Mr. M. Conway, M.P. for North Antrim; Mr. D. if French, Q.C., the Liberal candidate at the last election in the Newton Division -, Mr. C. M. Percy, Messrs. John Prescott, M. Birkhead, L. T. Foulkes, J. Newton, P. Thompson, G. Ratcliffe, T. Morris (Earlestown), W. D. Burdis, W. Urquhart„ A. J. Rawlinson (Newton), J. Taylor (llaydock), F. A. R. Neill (Bold), F. Broad- bridge, W. C. Rawlins, Jas. Tyson, Pierce Mahoney, Keegan, Thomas Flood, and others. The Chairman announced that he had received several letters apologising for non-attendance, Mr. E. R. Russell, M.P., wrote: "April 19th, 1887. Dear Mr. Rawlins,—l only wish I could be present with you, on Saturday, to join in the hearty and unani- mous protest which I am sure the Liberals of Earlestown will make against the abominable bill now passing through Parliameht. There may still be some hope that public demonstrations will check the career of the measure. If not we shall always be able to reflect with pride that we have with the greatest zeal protested against so retregrade an attempt to assail the liberties of the people. I am, yours faithfully, EDWARD a. RIISSELL."—The following letter had been re- ceived !lima Mr. E. K. Muspratt :—" Liverpool, 21 April, IBB7.—Dear Mr. Rawlins,—l am going to London to-day, and shall not he back in time to take part in your anti- coercion meeting at Earlestown ; otherwise I should have been very glad to have been present to protest against the infamous bill for the suppression of political agitation in Ireland. now before Parliament. I hope you will have a good meeting, and that the meats tactics of the Tories and Liberal dissentients in abusing their political opponents, and attempting to associate them with murder will be ex- posed.—Yours faithfully, EDMUND K. MIISPRATT."—Other communications had been received from Mr. T. S. Little, Mr. William Crosfield, and a telegram from Mr. T. P. O'Con- nor. Proceeding the Chairman stated they were met that 'night in a great political crisis. The Government had in their infinite wisdom thought it necessary to being in a Criminal Law Amendment Bill, or what they called a Coer- cion Bill, for Ireland, and they had the criticisms of their grand old leader. Mr. GI idstope(applause)—who had, so to speak, "doubled up" the Government into a cocked hat. (Laughter and applause.) At all event, they had never attempted to answer his criticisms. They all knew the second reading of the bill was a thing of the past, and they had only to look to the Committee stages of the House of Commons for the means of taking away the sting of the bill and to attend it. Under those circumstances the Liberals of the Newton Division had thought it their duty to meet together and to protest in a way that could not be mistaken against the iniquitous bill. (Applause.) He remarked that the position of the Liberal dissentients was a very grave one, and said they would hove to account for their action to the constituencies. Former coercion measures had been supported by the majoritp of the Irish members, and by the bulk of the. Scotch, Welsh, and, English Liberals and Conservatives alike, but now the great bulk of the Irish people, as represented by their members in the House of Commons, were dead against coercion, they found that Scotland was against coercion; that Wales was also against coercion, and that a very large minority of Englaerd was against coercion, a minority that was increasing every day. (Applause) Mr. John Prescott, Earleatown, moved—" That this meet- ing of the electors of Newton Division of South-West Lan- cashire records its continued and unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone aad his colleagues, and trusts his efforts to give justice to Ireland will be crowned with success." (Ap- plause.) He said he could not help sympathising with their great leader in the work which he had undertaken. During the last few months he had been led to ask the question, how was it that a man who held the reins of power in this mighty empire, who stood head and shoulders above his fellows, a man who had a majority assured, should deliber- ately sacrifice his position for oppressed Ireland. (Ap- plauee.) The only conclusion he could come to was that the man who had sympathised with oppressed Greece, who had spoken out boldly in her favour ; the same illustrious statesman who had spoken nobly in favour of Italian inde- pendence, and nobly supported the oppressed nationalities of Southern Europe, this man could not help—when the suffer- ings of Ireland were presented to his notice—he could not help his whole soul going out in one grand and gigantic

CAPSIZING OF A BOAT.—FOUR LIVES LOST—An inquest was held at Walton-on-thc Naze, on Tuarday, touching the circumstances attending a beating accident, whereby four men lost their lives. The deceased, whose names are Batchelor, Rick, Blackwell, and Osborne—the two latter be- longing to London—went out in a small boat, on Saturday night, with the intention of taking the craft round from the backwater to the sea front, in readiners for a trip to Harwich next day. Early the following morning, a woman saw a boat, bottom upwardr, on the b2ach, and, on rearch being made, the dead belies of Batchelor and Blackwell were found, entangle) in the sails and rigging.
